meta.title: CrashFree India — State Road-Safety Governance Dataset
meta.description: Consolidated dataset merging 12 state-level road-safety governance and key-individual research files, each independently self-audited (fresh-search re-derivation + active disconfirming-evidence search) per research-rules.md. Every source citation from the original files is preserved. Every fact still flagged as UNVERIFIED / LIKELY STALE / PARTIALLY VERIFIED after the audit is carried forward here as a structured 'flag' object (badge) rather than prose, for direct rendering in a dashboard UI.

flag_resolution_category_key.a: A genuine, documented second/third attempt was made (≥2 search angles) but could not surface 2 independent corroborating sources.
flag_resolution_category_key.b: The ambiguity is genuinely unresolved in present-day reality (e.g. a contested jurisdiction, an active court stay, a transfer too recent to be reflected in any published source).

state_files.rajasthan: (added as 13th pilot state, 25 Sept 2026 — no original .md file; researched directly into this schema)

notable_corrections.summary: Deputy CM Ajit Pawar had died (28 Jan 2026) and was still listed as a serving minister — the single most significant correction across all 12 files.
The file's claim that no PWD Minister of State existed was a factual error — Brijesh Singh has held the post continuously since 2022.
The Road Construction Minister's name ("Kumar Dhirendra") did not match any source and was corrected to Kumar Shailendra; the Patna DM (who chairs the city's Road Safety Committee) had been replaced.
An active ED money-laundering investigation into the sitting PWD Minister, breaking two days before this audit, was entirely new information with direct bearing on CrashFree India's engagement plan.
Active, unresolved High Court litigation over the removal of the HYDRAA Commissioner was likewise new and directly relevant.
Resolved a standing priority question (whether the 2017 Road Safety Authority Bill was enacted) that determines which governance-model category the state belongs to.

tamil_nadu.political_context: Tamil Nadu held Legislative Assembly elections in 2026, with polling on 23 April 2026 and results on 4 May 2026. In a historic upset, the newly formed Tamilaga Vettri Kazhagam (TVK), led by actor C. Joseph Vijay ("Vijay"), emerged as the single largest party with 108 of 234 seats — short of a majority, producing Tamil Nadu's first hung assembly. TVK formed a coalition government with Congress and other partners' support, and Vijay was sworn in as Chief Minister on 10 May 2026, ending the DMK's M. K. Stalin government; Stalin himself lost his own seat, the first incumbent CM to lose a TN election since Jayalalithaa in 1996. Any reference to a DMK-era minister or to "Chief Minister Stalin" is now historical only. CM Vijay personally retains Home/Police, General Administration, Municipal Administration, Urban and Water Supply, and several welfare portfolios — a structural pattern similar to Bihar/Jharkhand CMs who personally hold road-safety-adjacent departments. The cabinet sworn in on 10 May 2026 assigned Public Works (Buildings, Highways and Minor Ports) and Sports Development to Aadhav Arjuna; Transport to Vijay Tamilan Parthiban (who formally assumed the portfolio on 21 May 2026, per his own biography, distinct from the 10 May general oath date); Revenue and Disaster Management to K. A. Sengottaiyan; Rural Development and Water Resources to N. Anand; Health, Medical Education and Family Welfare to Dr. K. G. Arunraj; and Housing and Urban Development to B. Rajkumar. Dr. M. Sai Kumar, IAS continues as Chief Secretary, having been granted a further six-month service extension (1 September 2026 – 28 February 2027) under Rule 16(1) of the AIS (DCRB) Rules, 1958, ahead of his original 31 August 2026 retirement date; Dr. P. Senthilkumar serves as Additional Chief Secretary/Secretary-I to the CM and G. Laxmi Priya as Secretary-II to the CM (this last detail sourced only to Elets eGov and not independently re-corroborated in this pass). (Election/succession sources: Wikipedia — 2026 Tamil Nadu Legislative Assembly election, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2026_Tamil_Nadu_Legislative_Assembly_election; Wikipedia — M. K. Stalin, https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M._K._Stalin.)

governance_bodies.name: Tamil Nadu Road Safety Policy (2007) and State Road Safety Machinery
governance_bodies.mandate: Tamil Nadu's Road Safety Policy dates to April 2007, making it, per its own framing, the first state-level road safety policy in India, predating the National Road Safety Policy (2010). Thrust areas: Engineering, Enforcement, and Education, plus data collection, safe infrastructure, driver safety, and Emergency Medical Response. The policy itself is not a legislative Act — no specific statutory reference was found, consistent with the MV Act Section 215 executive-rules model seen in Bihar/Jharkhand rather than Karnataka's dedicated 2017 Act.
governance_bodies.roads_owned: Not applicable — a policy framework, not a road-owning body.
governance_bodies.hierarchy: The 2007 policy proposed establishing a "lead agency" (a Road Safety Authority), but CAG's own analysis found the policy document does not detail that body's composition, chair, or meeting frequency, nor does it specify a dedicated road-safety budget/fund — a documented, independently-flagged gap in Tamil Nadu's own road-safety governance design.
governance_bodies.subordinate_bodies: District Road Safety Committees (DRSCs) — confirmed to exist at district level (e.g., Tirupathur district's own government portal lists a DRSC page), consistent with the national MV Act s.215(3) template, but composition, chair, and meeting frequency could not be independently fetched/confirmed in this pass (the district page itself returned a fetch error) — flagged as a priority gap.
governance_bodies.decision_making_power: Not established from the sources reviewed (Road Safety Authority/lead agency composition, chair, and meeting frequency not detailed in the policy itself).
governance_bodies.data_role: Data collection is named as one of the policy's thrust areas, but no dedicated statewide data mechanism is detailed in sources reviewed.
governance_bodies.performance_issues: Citizen consumer and civic Action Group (CAG), a Chennai-based consumer/civic NGO (distinct from the Comptroller and Auditor General), has run District Road Safety Conferences in multiple districts (Salem, Madurai, Cuddalore) and an annual Road Safety Week press campaign, indicating an active civil-society engagement channel with DRSCs — but statewide DRSC composition and cadence remain unconfirmed.
governance_bodies.meeting_frequency: Not independently confirmed in this pass (Tirupathur DRSC page fetch blocked; no statewide DRSC roster located).

governance_bodies.decision_making_power: For CrashFree India, IIT Madras' Centre of Excellence for Road Safety / RBG Labs is Tamil Nadu's closest analogue to NIMHANS in Karnataka — a technically credible, already-active research and data partner with a working relationship to Greater Chennai Traffic Police specifically, making it a strong first technical-partnership target rather than a purely political one.
governance_bodies.data_role: RBG Labs built the crash-data dashboard underlying the national iRAD system. In January 2026, this dashboard was reported as adopted by Odisha (integrating police/officials and citizen accident-reporting portals), with plans for pan-India expansion.

governance_bodies.meeting_frequency: Runs recurring, dated public programmes: "Road Safety Month 2024," a "Principals' Conclave" under "Training Young Minds," a recurring "Zero Accident Day" campaign with Greater Chennai Traffic Police, and an ongoing SNS Foundation research partnership.

delhi.political_context: Delhi is not a full state but a Union Territory with a Legislative Assembly (National Capital Territory of Delhi), governed under Article 239AA of the Constitution and the Government of National Capital Territory of Delhi Act, 1991. Police, Public Order, and Land are constitutionally excluded from the Delhi government's legislative and executive domain and remain with the Union Government acting through the Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA) -- Delhi Police does not report to the Delhi Chief Minister or any Delhi minister at all, and its Commissioner is appointed directly by MHA order (confirmed by the MHA appointment order for Anurag Kumar, IPS, effective 17 July 2026, which also directed his predecessor to report to the Lieutenant Governor pending reposting). A 2023 amendment to the GNCTD Act (upheld in substance after the Supreme Court's 2023 Delhi services judgment prompted it) further gave the Lieutenant Governor sole discretionary authority, taking precedence over the Council of Ministers, on Delhi-Centre relations and on civil-service transfers/postings recommended by the National Capital Civil Services Authority -- meaning the LG is not a ceremonial figure in Delhi's governance in the way a Governor typically is in a full state. The Municipal Corporation of Delhi (MCD) layers a second executive duality on top of this: an elected, politically accountable Mayor (currently BJP's Pravesh Wahi) sits alongside a centrally posted IAS Municipal Commissioner (currently Sanjeev Khirwar) who holds the actual day-to-day executive and licensing/demolition authority -- a split that became acutely visible in September 2026 when a fatal Satya Niketan building collapse (seven dead) triggered public resignation demands directed at the Commissioner specifically, not the Mayor. In 2025-2026 all four apex offices changed hands: the BJP's Rekha Gupta became Chief Minister on 20 February 2025, ending a decade of AAP government under Arvind Kejriwal/Atishi; Vinai Kumar Saxena, LG since 2022, was moved to become LG of Ladakh and former career diplomat (and former Ambassador to the United States) Taranjit Singh Sandhu was sworn in as the new LG of Delhi on 11 March 2026, still in office as of this research pass (25 September 2026); BJP's Pravesh Wahi was elected Mayor of the MCD on 29 April 2026 with 156 of 165 votes cast, succeeding Raja Iqbal Singh (BJP, Apr 2025-Apr 2026), who had succeeded Mahesh Kumar Khichi (AAP, Nov 2024-Apr 2025) -- the point at which mayoral control passed from AAP to BJP; and Anurag Kumar, IPS (1994-batch, AGMUT cadre, a career intelligence officer previously Special Director of the Intelligence Bureau) was appointed Commissioner of Delhi Police on 17 July 2026, replacing Satish Golcha. Below the Commissioner, Delhi Police's Traffic Management Division -- the unit CrashFree India would work with on enforcement -- changed hands again in a Commissioner-ordered reshuffle of 43 IPS/DANIPS officers on 19 August 2026 (timed ahead of the 18th BRICS Summit, 12-13 September 2026), which returned 1996-batch IPS officer Ajay Chaudhary to head Traffic. On the elected side, the Legislative Assembly itself is lopsided (48 BJP to 22 AAP in the 8th Delhi Assembly), with former Chief Minister Atishi serving as Leader of the Opposition since February 2025. Practically, any Delhi engagement strategy must run on at least three separate, only partly overlapping tracks -- the elected Delhi government (PWD, Transport, MCD-adjacent civic matters), the Union-controlled Delhi Police/MHA enforcement track, and the MCD's own elected-Mayor/centrally-posted-Commissioner split -- with the Lieutenant Governor sitting institutionally above all three on several matters. This is a structure materially different from every full state in this document set, and CrashFree India asks that bundle enforcement, infrastructure, and civic-body commitments into a single proposal risk addressing an office that cannot actually deliver all three.

governance_bodies.name: Delhi Police (incl. Delhi Traffic Police) — a Union subject, not a Delhi government department
governance_bodies.mandate: Law enforcement, public order, and traffic policing in Delhi, including via a dedicated Traffic Management Division/Traffic Police wing.
governance_bodies.roads_owned: Not a road-owning body; holds enforcement authority over traffic on all Delhi roads regardless of the owning body (PWD, MCD, NDMC, Cantonment, or NHAI).
governance_bodies.hierarchy: Reports to the Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA), Government of India — NOT to the Delhi Chief Minister, any Delhi government minister, or a Delhi "Home Department" (no such department has operational authority over Delhi Police). This follows from Article 239AA of the Constitution and the Government of National Capital Territory of Delhi Act, 1991, under which Police, Public Order, and Land are constitutionally excluded from the Delhi government's legislative and executive domain. The Supreme Court's May 2023 Constitution Bench ruling (in the NCTD-vs-Union "Services" case) confirmed the LG's own discretionary powers extend only to these three excluded subjects (plus matters the President specifically delegates); the Government of NCT of Delhi (Amendment) Act, 2023 subsequently created the National Capital Civil Services Authority (NCCSA) to route transfer/posting decisions for other services through the LG, layering a further Union check onto the bureaucracy even outside Police/Land/Public Order. The Home Ministry has previously and explicitly rejected proposals to place a Traffic wing under the Delhi government.
governance_bodies.subordinate_bodies: Traffic Management Division/Traffic Police wing under a Special Commissioner of Police (Traffic), with a Joint Commissioner of Police (Traffic) as operational head beneath that tier and DCP (Traffic) posts below; DANIPS/IPS officer cadre subject to periodic MHA-ordered reshuffles. The exact reporting relationship between the Special CP (Traffic) and Joint CP (Traffic) posts was not independently confirmed with an official org chart in this pass (traffic.delhipolice.gov.in's detailed structure page was not fetchable).

governance_bodies.name: Municipal Corporation of Delhi (MCD)

governance_bodies.roads_owned: Owns and maintains local roads, footpaths, streetlights, and drains outside the NDMC and Delhi Cantonment areas; covers roughly 94% of Delhi's area, organised into administrative zones (12 zones, per the December 2025 revenue-district reorganisation that explicitly aligned Delhi's new 13 revenue districts with "the 12 administrative zones of the Municipal Corporation of Delhi (MCD), the New Delhi Municipal Council (NDMC), and the Delhi Cantonment").

governance_bodies.mandate: A dedicated multi-agency transport-planning and road-safety coordination body for the whole of the NCT of Delhi, established by DDA via a Gazette of India notification (S.O. governance_bodies.name: Office of the Lieutenant Governor (LG) of Delhi / Raj Niwas
governance_bodies.mandate: Constitutional office representing the Union Government in the NCT of Delhi under Article 239AA, created by the Constitution (Sixty-ninth Amendment) Act, 1991. The LG is required to act on the aid and advice of the Delhi Council of Ministers EXCEPT on matters (a) beyond the Delhi Legislative Assembly's competence — Public Order, Police and Land, which are excluded from the Assembly's law-making power entirely — and (b) other matters where the President has specifically delegated discretionary power to the LG (post-2023, this includes recommendations of the National Capital Civil Services Authority on transfers/postings/vigilance for Delhi's civil services).
governance_bodies.roads_owned: Not a road-owning body directly, but chairs both DDA and UTTIPEC (see those entries) — the institutions holding Union land-use authority over road-network layout and multi-agency transport-infrastructure approval for Delhi — giving the LG's office an outsized institutional role in Delhi road planning despite not being an elected part of the road-owning agencies themselves.
governance_bodies.hierarchy: Apex representative of the Union Government within Delhi's governance structure; sits institutionally above the elected CM/Council of Ministers on the three excluded subjects, chairs the DDA and (via DDA) UTTIPEC, and is the appointing/administrative-control authority (through the Ministry of Home Affairs) for Delhi Police, NDMC's Chairperson, and MCD's Commissioner, even though NDMC formally reports to MoHUA and MCD is a separately elected body.
governance_bodies.subordinate_bodies: Not applicable in the usual departmental sense; the LG's office coordinates across DDA, UTTIPEC, and (via MHA) Delhi Police, NDMC, and civil-service postings through the National Capital Civil Services Authority (NCCSA), created by the Government of NCT of Delhi (Amendment) Act, 2023.

Administrative control over Delhi Police, NDMC leadership, MCD's Commissioner, and (via NCCSA) postings across the wider Delhi civil service flows through the LG's office and MHA rather than the elected Delhi government.
governance_bodies.data_role: Not detailed in any source reviewed.
governance_bodies.performance_issues: The single most consequential structural fact for CrashFree India's Delhi engagement: the LG's office, not the elected CM/Transport Minister, sits atop the enforcement (Police) and much of the planning-approval (DDA/UTTIPEC) tracks, while the elected government controls engineering execution (PWD) and licensing (Transport Dept). Any Delhi road-safety intervention that needs both engineering change AND enforcement/planning sign-off may require engaging both tracks separately.
governance_bodies.meeting_frequency: Not specified in any source reviewed.

governance_bodies.name: Ministry of Home Affairs (MHA), Government of India — Delhi Division
governance_bodies.mandate: The Union ministry exercising direct executive control over Police, Public Order, and (via DANICS/AGMUT cadre administration and the LG) Land and Services in the NCT of Delhi — the three subjects Article 239AA excludes from the elected Delhi government's domain, plus, since the 2023 amendment, a wider role in transfers/postings for Delhi's civil services generally.
governance_bodies.roads_owned: Not a road-owning body; relevant to CrashFree India because it is the actual appointing/reporting authority for Delhi Police (including Traffic Police), and — through Union appointment of AGMUT-cadre IAS officers — for MCD's Commissioner and NDMC's Chairperson as well, even though those two bodies formally report to MoHUA rather than MHA on other matters.
governance_bodies.hierarchy: Union Cabinet-level ministry; the Delhi Police Commissioner, Special/Joint Commissioners of Police, and DCPs are all MHA/AGMUT-cadre appointments and postings, publicly announced via MHA orders rather than Delhi government notifications.
governance_bodies.subordinate_bodies: Delhi Police (operational command); National Capital Civil Services Authority (NCCSA), created by the 2023 GNCTD Amendment Act to recommend transfer/posting/vigilance decisions for Delhi's civil services to the LG.
governance_bodies.decision_making_power: Appoints and transfers the Delhi Police Commissioner and all senior Traffic Police leadership; the Home Ministry has explicitly and on the record rejected past proposals to place a Traffic wing under the Delhi government, underscoring that this is a settled, not contested-in-practice, division of authority.
governance_bodies.data_role: Not detailed in any source reviewed.
governance_bodies.performance_issues: Because MHA's role is exercised almost entirely through officer appointments/transfers rather than a visible standing "Delhi Division" office that CrashFree India could approach directly, the practical engagement point for anything requiring MHA sign-off is the Delhi Police Commissioner's office itself, not a separate ministry desk.

governance_bodies.hierarchy: Political head held personally by CM Rekha Gupta; as of 1 January 2026, restructured from 11 to 13 revenue districts (dissolving Shahdara district and creating Old Delhi, Central North, and Outer North districts), each headed by a Deputy Commissioner who also serves as District Magistrate, with 39 sub-divisions (up from 33/22 depending on the source's baseline) each headed by a Sub-Divisional Magistrate (SDM). madhya_pradesh.political_context: Dr. Mohan Yadav (BJP) has served as Chief Minister of Madhya Pradesh since 13 December 2023, with Rajendra Shukla and Jagdish Devda as Deputy Chief Ministers (Wikipedia — Mohan Yadav: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mohan_Yadav). The cabinet was sworn in and portfolios allocated on 25/30 December 2023, and a fresh 11 September 2026 re-audit independently re-confirmed all six road-safety-relevant portfolios directly against each minister's own Wikipedia biography, finding them unchanged apart from one narrow, dated exception: on 16 July 2026 the Animal Husbandry and Dairy Development portfolio was withdrawn from Minister of State Lakhan Patel and placed directly under the Chief Minister in a late-night notification (Goemkarponn, 16 July 2026: https://goemkarponn.com/late-night-portfolio-change-sparks-buzz-over-cabinet-reshuffle-in-madhya-pradesh/); that reshuffle does not touch any of the six road-safety-relevant portfolios. Separately, a Dainik Jagran (Madhya Pradesh) report circulating in 2026 discusses speculation about a larger cabinet reshuffle — triggered by Urban Development Minister Kailash Vijayvargiya's political standing after the Dec 2025-Jan 2026 Bhagirathpura (Indore) contaminated-water tragedy — naming Vijayvargiya, Prahlad Singh Patel, Dilip Ahirwar, and Radha Singh as ministers who "could" see portfolios changed, while explicitly stating "no official confirmation has come from the CM's office" and floating a possible window no earlier than mid-2026 (Dainik Jagran English: https://english.dainikjagranmpcg.com/states/madhya-pradesh/seo-headline-mp-cabinet-reshuffle-2026-mohan-yadav-eyes-ministry/article-15391). As of the research date (11 September 2026) no such reshuffle has occurred and both ministers' Wikipedia pages still show their December 2023 portfolios, but Vijayvargiya's and Patel's portfolios should be treated as most at near-term risk of change and reconfirmed before any high-stakes outreach. CM Mohan Yadav personally retains General Administration, Home, Jail, and Industrial Policy and Investment Promotion, meaning — as in Bihar, Jharkhand, and Tamil Nadu — the Chief Minister personally controls the police/enforcement chain, a recurring structural pattern across states in this document set. The DGP is Kailash Makwana, IPS (1988-batch), appointed 1 December 2024 by Home Department order dated 23 November 2024, originally due to retire December 2025 but extended to December 2026 under Supreme Court two-year-minimum-tenure guidelines; a fresh 11 September 2026 re-check found no replacement, resignation, or transfer, so his tenure through December 2026 stands reconfirmed.

source_audit: The full December 2023 cabinet portfolio list was originally sourced to a single news article (India TV News). This pass independently re-verified all six road-safety-relevant ministers plus the CM directly against each individual's own Wikipedia biography (Rakesh Singh, Uday Pratap Singh, Kailash Vijayvargiya, Prahlad Singh Patel, Rajendra Shukla, Karan Singh Verma) and found every one still current as of this research date — the list is now Verified, not LIKELY STALE-adjacent, though Vijayvargiya and Patel are flagged as exposed to active (unconfirmed) reshuffle speculation reported by Dainik Jagran, and the confirmed narrow July 2026 portfolio change (Animal Husbandry, Minister of State Lakhan Patel) remains a reminder that individual reassignments can happen without notice.

The Zero Fatality Mission's nine-district scope and directives, originally a single-source finding, are now cross-checked against a second, independent outlet (Free Press Journal, 31 August 2026, in addition to the original 2 September 2026 article) reporting the same expansion event with consistent core facts — upgraded to Verified, Moderate-High Confidence. A fresh search for any further district additions since 2 September 2026 found none as of 11 September 2026.

The Madhya Pradesh Transport Commissioner (Umesh Joga, since ~29 January 2026) and the Bhopal (Sanjay Kumar) and Indore (Santosh Kumar Singh) Police Commissioners were newly identified and cross-checked against two sources each (The Print / IndianBureaucracy.com for Joga and Kumar; the Indore Commissionerate's own site plus Free Press Journal for Singh) — these were priority gaps in the prior version, now resolved.

The Bhopal (Malti Rai, since July 2022) and Indore (Pushyamitra Bhargav, since 2022) mayors were newly identified — Bhopal corroborated by two sources, Indore by one strong source (Wikipedia) — resolving a previously flagged gap.
Madhya Pradesh's district count (55) is now confirmed against a specific, cited source rather than left as an unverified 'widely reported' figure.

District Road Safety Committee composition and chair for Madhya Pradesh specifically remain inferred by strong analogy to the national SCCoRS template and to the pattern independently confirmed in Bihar, Karnataka, and Jharkhand — not confirmed via a Madhya-Pradesh-specific primary document; this pass did not find a working, fetchable copy of the Khargone DRSC notice either, so this remains Partially Verified, criterion (a): a documented, repeated attempt has failed to surface a primary MP-specific DRSC charter or notification.

assam.political_context: Assam held Legislative Assembly elections in 2026, and Himanta Biswa Sarma (BJP) was returned for a second term as Chief Minister, with the Second Sarma ministry sworn in on 12 May 2026 (initial CM-plus-four ceremony) followed by a full cabinet expansion to 17 ministers (14 BJP, 2 AGP, 1 BPF) confirmed by 16 June 2026. Assam's Second Sarma ministry has NO Deputy Chief Minister -- a genuine structural feature (re-checked this pass; no source names one), unlike Bihar or several other states in this document series, meaning there is no 'number two' political figure to route outreach through. CM Sarma personally holds an unusually concentrated set of portfolios directly relevant to road safety: Home (except Prisons, Home Guards), Personnel, Public Works (Buildings & National Highways), Public Works (Roads), and -- per the state's own cabinet-list sources -- Medical Education & Research, though a later (16 June 2026) independent tabulation instead lists Medical Education & Research under Health Minister Ashok Singhal; this discrepancy is unresolved and flagged. This gives one office simultaneous control of enforcement (Home/Police), road engineering (both PWD wings), and the state's Road Safety Council chairmanship (ex officio, by virtue of being CM). Other road-safety-relevant portfolios: Transport & Welfare of Bodoland (Charan Boro, BPF), Health & Family Welfare (Ashok Singhal, BJP, also ex officio GMDA Chairperson), Finance, Environment & Forest, Mines & Minerals (Jayanta Mallabaruah, BJP, since 5 June 2026 -- Finance is the ex officio-adjacent portfolio relevant to the Assam Road Safety Fund's cess and grant flows, though the Fund Management Committee itself is chaired by the Chief Secretary, not the Finance Minister), Revenue & Disaster Management (Keshab Mahanta, AGP), and Panchayat & Rural Development / Implementation of Assam Accord / Excise / Border Protection & Development (Atul Bora, AGP). Dr. Ravi Kota, IAS (1993 batch) is Chief Secretary, in the post since 17 January 2024 with his tenure formally extended by six months beyond superannuation, from 1 May 2026 to 31 October 2026 -- meaning a Chief Secretary transition is likely within weeks of this research date (25 September 2026) and any CFI relationship-building with his office should anticipate a successor. Kota has a genuine, dated road-safety track record: on 29 April 2026 he chaired a statewide road-safety review (Q1 2026 data: 4,219 accidents, 1,008 fatalities, nine districts accounting for ~50% of fatalities), directed NHAI/NHIDCL/PWD suo motu action on black spots, and explicitly urged districts to draw on Road Safety Fund money and partner with NGOs on signage -- a direct, documented opening for CrashFree India. Harmeet Singh, IPS (1992-batch, Assam-Meghalaya cadre) remains DGP, re-confirmed current by an official Assam Police directory dated 19 August 2026 (the most current dated primary source located this pass, superseding the January/March 2026 snapshots used previously). The same 19 August 2026 directory resolves a prior flag with strong, current, official corroboration: Dr. P.S. Mahanta, IPS (2007-batch, promotee) holds three concurrent titles -- Commissioner of Police, Guwahati; IGP (Traffic & Road Safety), Assam; and Chief of the State Task Force -- and Jayanta Sarathi Borah, APS is confirmed as DCP (Traffic), Guwahati Commissionerate. A separate IGP (BTAD), Bijoy Giri Kuligam, IPS, heads policing specifically in the Bodoland Territorial Area Districts. This pass also confirms a genuinely current (as of 25 September 2026), still-pending Gauhati High Court road-safety PIL -- Gaurav Dey vs. The State of Assam & 7 Ors, PIL/31/2026 -- filed by a Guwahati law student challenging the absence of safety regulation (blind-spot mitigation, 360-degree cameras, speed limiters, operating-hours restrictions) for dumper/tipper trucks, naming the Transport Department, police authorities, the Regional Transport Officer, MoRTH, and vehicle manufacturers Tata Motors and Ashok Leyland as respondents; the case was last heard 15 September 2026 and adjourned to 16 November 2026. This resolves the prior 'no current PIL found' gap and gives CrashFree India both a live litigation to track and a genuine, documented individual road-safety champion (Gaurav Dey) outside government. A second, independent documented road-safety champion was found: Bhupen Borah, BJP MLA for Bihpuria, publicly urged the state government and police (3 June 2026) to seize motorcycles for a month and impose age-based speed restrictions on young riders after fatal helmetless-riding accidents in his constituency -- he should not be confused with the differently-spelled Congress leader/former APCC president of a similar name, a distinction worth flagging for CFI staff. Devajit (Lon) Saikia was re-appointed Advocate General of Assam for a second five-year term on 13 May 2026 (having resigned 6 May 2026 per constitutional convention when the outgoing government's term ended) -- relevant given his office's institutional role in defending the state in PIL/31/2026 and any future road/bridge litigation. The Leader of the Opposition in the Assam Legislative Assembly is Wazed Ali Choudhury (INC), who assumed the position on 27 May 2026 (Deputy Leader: Joy Prakash Das, INC). A genuinely distinct institutional wrinkle this pass investigated in depth, per the client's specific request: the Bodoland Territorial Region (BTR/BTC) runs its own parallel road-governance structure for its constituent districts (Kokrajhar, Chirang, Baksa, Udalguri, Tamulpur), separate from the state PWRD/Transport Department chain of command that governs the rest of Assam. Following BTC's own September 2025 council election (won outright by the Bodoland People's Front, 28 of 40 seats) and a 28 November 2025 portfolio reallocation, BTC Chief Executive Member Hagrama Mohilary (BPF) personally holds PWD, Panchayat & Rural Development, and Finance within BTC (mirroring, at the sub-state level, the same pattern of one office concentrating road-engineering and fiscal control seen with CM Sarma at the state level), while BTC Executive Member Mritunjoy Narzary holds the Transport portfolio within BTC. Notably, Charan Boro -- the state's own Transport Minister -- and Hagrama Mohilary belong to the same party (BPF), which currently controls both the state Transport portfolio and the entirety of BTC's executive, a genuine and useful political alignment for any CrashFree India engagement strategy that needs to work across the BTAD boundary. India's Seventh Schedule splits road-related subjects across the Union and State Lists (roads, transport and police sit substantially on the State List, with the Union retaining National Highways, the Motor Vehicles Act framework, and centrally sponsored schemes like PMGSY), so Assam's state government -- and, within BTAD specifically, the BTC executive -- are the primary points of leverage for nearly all road-safety interventions CrashFree India will pursue.

governance_bodies.name: Public Works (Roads) Department (PWRD), Government of Assam
governance_bodies.mandate: "To develop and maintain the state road infrastructure for providing connectivity and efficient transportation" — planning, construction and maintenance of roads, bridges and culverts. Uniquely among the states in this document series, PWRD's own site frames its remit as covering State Highways, Major District Roads AND PMGSY rural connectivity together, rather than splitting rural roads into a separate department; Assam does not operate a distinct "Rural Works Department" of the Bihar/Jharkhand type — confirmed in this pass via a district-level cross-check (Chirang district's PWD (R&B) Division page explicitly lists PMGSY, CMGSY and NESIDS among its own funded programmes).
governance_bodies.roads_owned: State Highways (SH), Major District Roads (MDR), Other District Roads (ODR), Village Roads (VR) and PMGSY rural-connectivity roads statewide, through one department rather than a separate rural-works body.
governance_bodies.hierarchy: Political head held personally by CM Himanta Biswa Sarma. Administrative head: Secretary to the Government of Assam, PWRD (Debajit Das, per the department's own current contact page), with a Commissioner & Special Secretary (Sanjiv Shyam), a Special Commissioner (Bibhuti Saikia) and a Special Secretary (Debajit Bhuyan) below him. Engineering head: Chief Engineer, PWD (Roads) (in-charge: Hemanta Dewri Bharali), alongside separate Chief Engineers for Border Roads & NEC Works (Rati Kanta Pegu) and for Externally Aided Projects/EAP (Jewel Timung). Below the Chief Engineers, the department runs six geographic zones, each under an Additional Chief Engineer: Eastern Zone (HQ Dibrugarh), Tezpur Zone (HQ Tezpur), Diphu Zone, Haflong Zone, a dedicated "BTC Zone" (HQ Kokrajhar, covering the Bodoland Territorial Region), and Barak Valley (HQ Silchar) — 23 Circle offices sit below the zones (e.g. Kokrajhar (R&B) Circle, HQ Kokrajhar).
governance_bodies.subordinate_bodies: Assam Road Research and Training Institute (ARRTI); Assam State Road Board (ASRB, which administers the Assam Road Maintenance Fund and helps implement PMGSY); the department also operates a separate PMGSY Maintenance Branch ("eMARG") for periodic renewal of already-built PMGSY roads.

governance_bodies.name: Bodoland Territorial Council (BTC) / Bodoland Territorial Region (BTR) — PWD & road authority under the Sixth Schedule
governance_bodies.mandate: BTC is a Sixth-Schedule autonomous self-governing body for the Bodoland Territorial Region (BTAD), covering the districts of Kokrajhar, Chirang, Baksa and Udalguri, created by the 10 February 2003 Memorandum of Settlement among the Government of India, Government of Assam and the Bodo Liberation Tigers, and given constitutional protection under the Sixth Schedule to the Constitution. "PWD" is listed as item 5 of 40 subjects the 2003 accord specifies as being "entrusted to BTC by [the] Assam Government," alongside Transport (item 29) and Panchayat and Rural Development (item 12) as separate, also-transferred subjects. THIS SPECIFIC ATTRIBUTION RESTS ON THE PRIMARY ACCORD TEXT AS ARCHIVED BY THE UN PEACEMAKER TREATY DATABASE, NOT ON AN ASSAM GAZETTE OR PIB COPY: mha.gov.in and pib.gov.in pages on the Bodo Accord returned access errors (403) when checked directly in this pass, and this is flagged as a sourcing limitation rather than resolved.
governance_bodies.roads_owned: Nominally ambiguous, and this is the key structural finding for CrashFree India's outreach purposes: although "PWD" appears on the accord's list of subjects transferred to BTC, state PWRD's own official website confirms it continues to operate a full zonal engineering structure INSIDE the BTAD area — a dedicated "BTC Zone" (HQ Kokrajhar) under its own Additional Chief Engineer, with a "Kokrajhar (R&B) Circle" beneath it — and Chirang district's own government portal separately confirms a state-department "PWD (R&B) Division, Chirang," established 2008, running PMGSY/CMGSY/NESIDS-funded works from its headquarters at Kajolgaon, with no reference on that page to any separate BTC PWD authority. This indicates that, in practice, the Government of Assam's own PWRD/PWD(B&NH) continues to directly plan, execute and maintain State Highways, Major District Roads and PMGSY rural roads inside BTAD through its normal statewide zonal hierarchy, rather than having handed that engineering function wholesale to BTC. Separately, BTC does maintain its own PWD department (headquartered at the BTC Secretariat, Kokrajhar, per publicly listed BTC tender notices for road works), which appears to function alongside — not in place of — the state's Kokrajhar-zone PWRD/PWD offices, most plausibly for roads and works that fall outside the state's own road classification (SH/MDR/PMGSY) or for BTC's own locally-initiated development-plan works funded from its population-ratio-based grants-in-aid from the State Government.
governance_bodies.hierarchy: BTC has an Executive Council of up to 12 Executive Members (a Chief and Deputy Chief with Cabinet-Minister-equivalent status for protocol purposes in the BTC area), with executive functions exercised through a Principal Secretary (an officer not below Commissioner/Secretary rank in the Government of Assam) and, for delegated subjects such as PWD, a senior departmental officer who may be designated "Director of BTC" for that department. This BTC-side hierarchy sits alongside, not beneath, the state PWRD's own BTC Zone/Kokrajhar Circle chain of command described above.
governance_bodies.subordinate_bodies: BTC's own PWD Department (Kokrajhar); separately, and administratively distinct, the state PWRD's BTC Zone (Additional Chief Engineer, HQ Kokrajhar) and Kokrajhar (R&B) Circle, and the state PWD (R&B) Division, Chirang.
governance_bodies.decision_making_power: For CrashFree India's outreach purposes, the practical implication is that a road-safety problem inside the four BTAD districts cannot be assumed to fall under BTC's authority merely because "PWD" is nominally a nominally BTC-devolved subject: State Highways, Major District Roads and PMGSY roads within BTAD very plausibly remain under the state PWRD's own BTC-Zone/Kokrajhar-Circle chain (the same chain that reports to the Chief Engineer, PWD (Roads) and ultimately the CM as Minister, PWD (Roads)), while BTC's own PWD Department handles a separate, narrower set of works. Confirming which authority owns a specific road inside BTAD requires a direct, road-specific check before outreach — flagged explicitly as a research gap below.

governance_bodies.performance_issues: Not established from the sources reviewed; the general BTC road-infrastructure statistics available (2,680 gravelled roads, 2,650 blacktopped roads completed, and NH work in progress, per council-cited 2015–16-vintage figures) are now over a decade stale and are not included here as current data.

governance_bodies.name: Assam Road Safety Council
governance_bodies.mandate: Constituted under Motor Vehicles Act, 1988, Section 215 (enabling states to constitute road safety councils/committees), tasked with strengthening the institutional framework, building stakeholder-department capacity, strengthening enforcement and improving engineering measures. The Assam Road Safety Policy was notified by the Transport Department on 18 October 2016, following the Council's approval, and the Council itself approved the Assam Road Safety Action Plan (ARSAP) on 8 January 2015.
governance_bodies.roads_owned: Not applicable — a policy/coordination body, not a road-owning agency.
governance_bodies.hierarchy: Operates under the chairmanship of the Chief Minister of Assam — meaning, combined with the CM's personal hold on Home, PWD (Roads) and PWD (Buildings & NH), Assam's road-safety governance apex and its two largest road-owning departments currently sit with the same individual. Day-to-day coordination below the Council level runs through the Chief Secretary (see the 29 April 2026 review chaired by Dr. Ravi Kota) and the Transport Department.
governance_bodies.subordinate_bodies: District Road Safety Committees (DRSCs); the Assam Road Safety Fund's Fund Management Committee sits within the Transport Department rather than under the Council directly.

key_positions.title: Chair
key_positions.name: Chief Minister of Assam (Himanta Biswa Sarma, ex officio)
key_positions.confidence: Verified — High Confidence, sourced to the department's own current Road Safety page.

citation.label: pwdroads.assam.gov.in — Road Safety

governance_bodies.decision_making_power: Approves the state road safety policy and action plan; day-to-day enforcement of that plan visibly continues through Chief-Secretary-level reviews even where a formally-styled "Council" meeting has not been documented recently (see performance_issues).
governance_bodies.data_role: Not established from the sources reviewed.
governance_bodies.performance_issues: The Council's most recent meeting formally under that name remains the department's own cited 8 January 2015 date (approving ARSAP) — now over a decade stale, and no meeting formally styled as an "Assam Road Safety Council" meeting more recent than the 2016 policy notification was located in this or the prior pass. This should be read alongside clear, more recent evidence of active high-level coordination outside the Council's own name: a Chief-Secretary-chaired review on 29 April 2026 (ordering suo motu black-spot/junction action by NHAI, NHIDCL and PWD (NH), and directing districts to use Road Safety Funds and involve NGOs on signage) shows Assam's road-safety governance remains active in substance, even if the specific statutory "Council" has not visibly convened under its own name since 2016.
governance_bodies.meeting_frequency: No confirmed meeting under the Council's specific name since 2016; the State Road Safety Authority Bill, 2017 has NOT been enacted — it remained "under circulation for views and comments of stake holding Departments" as of the most recent department statement reviewed, placing Assam in the executive-rules governance-model category (alongside Bihar/Jharkhand) rather than a dedicated-statutory-Authority model (e.g. Karnataka's KSRSA).

haryana.political_context:
Nayab Singh Saini (BJP) has served as Chief Minister of Haryana since 12 March 2024 and was returned to office after the October 2024 Haryana Legislative Assembly election, with cabinet portfolios allocated on 21 October 2024. CM Saini personally holds roughly a dozen portfolios, including Home, Finance, Planning, Excise & Taxation, Town & Country Planning, Urban Estates, Housing, Criminal Investigation, and Law & Legislative -- a centralisation pattern seen in several other states in this research series -- though PWD and Transport sit with separate ministers. Haryana's Saini ministry has no Deputy Chief Minister (a structural difference from Bihar, Rajasthan and several other states researched in this series, all of which have one or more Deputy CMs); no source found in this pass names a Haryana Deputy CM for the 2024-2029 term. No cabinet reshuffle since October 2024 was found across this pass's searches (re-checked through September 2026), so the ministerial line-up first verified in the prior research pass -- Anil Vij (Transport, Energy, Labour), Ranbir Singh Gangwa (PWD Buildings & Roads, and Public Health Engineering), Vipul Goel (Revenue & Disaster Management, Urban Local Bodies), Krishan Lal Panwar (Development & Panchayats), and Arti Singh Rao (Health) -- is treated as still current, subject to the caveats noted on each minister's entry.

On the bureaucratic side, Anurag Rastogi, IAS continues as Chief Secretary and chairs the state's Fund Management Committee (FMC) on road safety; the state government sought (per The Print, 25 June 2026) a second one-year extension for him beyond his original 30 June 2025 retirement, through June 2027, citing administrative continuity. Sudhir Rajpal, IAS holds the Additional Chief Secretary, Home Department post and is the official who actually signs Haryana Police's transfer and reshuffle orders (confirmed as recently as an 11 July 2026 IPS reshuffle and referenced again around the 3 September 2026 reshuffle), since the Home Minister portfolio itself sits with the Chief Minister personally. The administrative bureaucracy is also under visible strain: as of the date of this research (25 September 2026), Haryana was reported running roughly 44 IAS officers short of its sanctioned strength, with several more retirements due before the end of 2026, including Arun Kumar Gupta -- who holds the dual charge of Principal Secretary to the Chief Minister and Finance Secretary -- due to retire on 30 September 2026 with no successor confirmed in this pass.

On policing, Ajay Singhal, IPS (1992-batch, an IIT Delhi mechanical-engineering graduate from Rewari) took charge as Haryana DGP on 1 January 2026, with a guaranteed minimum two-year tenure under the 2006 Prakash Singh Supreme Court judgment and a natural retirement date of 31 October 2028; he succeeded O.P. Singh, who had held interim charge after predecessor Shatrujeet Singh Kapur went on leave while named as an accused in an IPS officer's suicide case. Re-verification through the most recent Haryana IPS reshuffles found in this pass (11 July 2026 and 3 September 2026, the latter affecting 29 IPS and one HPS officer) confirmed Singhal remains DGP. Singhal has built a genuine, dated road-safety record distinct from routine departmental duty: on taking charge he set out a four-pillar strategy (engineering, enforcement, emergency medical response, awareness) and, by mid-January 2026, had launched an IIT-Madras-built 'Sanjaya' accident-mapping platform alongside a 'Baseline Survey' app tracking roughly 1,009 hospitals' trauma-care readiness, with a linked hospital performance-rating system tied to patient survival outcomes. His immediate predecessor as (interim) DGP, O.P. Singh, had separately written to the Union Ministry of Road Transport and Highways in November 2025 over 136 unaddressed black spots (of 474 identified statewide since 2019-20, with 223 rectified and 251 still pending), citing over 4,000 road-accident deaths in 2025 against roughly 800 homicides -- Singh's own words were that 'roads are now bigger killers.' Haryana's ADG, Traffic and Highways is currently Amitabh Singh Dhillon, IPS (1997-batch, Haryana cadre), who received the portfolio only as an additional charge (alongside ADGP Modernisation & Welfare and ADGP, Emergency Response Support System/112) in the 3 September 2026 reshuffle, succeeding Vikas Arora; his tenure is too fresh in this specific portfolio for an independent road-safety track record to be assessed.

On the civil side of the Transport Department, Prabhjot Singh, IAS was named Transport Commissioner and Secretary, Transport Department in an 8 August 2026 reshuffle of 17 IAS and 7 HCS officers, in addition to his existing charge as Director General, Environment and Secretary, Environment, Forests and Wildlife -- a dual charge, corroborated by both The Tribune's contemporaneous reshuffle coverage and the Transport Department's own website (hartrans.gov.in), which independently lists him in that role alongside Dhirendra Khadgata, IAS as Director, State Transport. The GMDA CEO gap flagged in the prior research pass is now resolved: Phool Chand ('P.C.') Meena, IAS is confirmed, via a 20 September 2026 Tribune interview (as GMDA CEO and dually as Municipal Corporation Gurugram Commissioner) discussing the authority's drainage and urban-flooding programme, to have returned to or remained in the GMDA CEO chair -- correcting the prior pass's inference that he had moved on to the Faridabad Metropolitan Development Authority; GMDA's own 9 September 2026 coordination-committee meeting under his chairmanship (on integrated road infrastructure) further corroborates his currency in the post as of this pass.

Haryana's Advocate General changed hands on 21 August 2026: Pawan Kumar Mutneja, a senior Punjab & Haryana High Court advocate (and Haryana's own Additional Advocate General from 1996-99), was appointed under Article 165(1) of the Constitution after predecessor Pravindra Kumar Chauhan was elevated to the High Court bench the same day; no specific, currently pending road/bridge-safety PIL naming him was identified in this pass, though the Punjab and Haryana High Court has a documented general history of hearing road-infrastructure PILs (for example, over incomplete roads/bridges in New Chandigarh, and a since-disposed PIL over a foot overbridge relocation on the Gurugram-Jaipur NH in Rewari district).

On the opposition side, Bhupinder Singh Hooda (INC), Chief Minister from 2005-2014, was named Leader of the Opposition in the Haryana Legislative Assembly around 29 September-3 October 2025. His public criticism of the Saini government since then has centred on general law-and-order and safety themes -- for example, citing the Centre's Social Progress Index to call Haryana 'the most unsafe state in the country' (Tribune, 8 August 2026) in the context of specific crime incidents -- rather than road safety specifically; no direct, on-the-record Hooda statement on road-accident policy was identified in this pass.

Haryana's NCR dimension: Gurugram and Faridabad (and parts of several other districts) fall inside the National Capital Region as defined by the National Capital Region Planning Board (NCRPB) Act, 1985, and the current Draft Regional Plan-2041 for NCR (a central, Ministry of Housing and Urban Affairs-linked body with Haryana government representation) does address regional road-network standards. In practice, however, this pass found the NCRPB's institutional footprint on Haryana's day-to-day road-safety governance to be indirect -- it is a regional land-use and infrastructure-planning coordination body, not an operational road-safety, funding, or enforcement authority. The concrete, name-able NCR-linked road-safety actor specific to Haryana is the Gurugram Metropolitan Development Authority (GMDA, a 2017 state statutory body, distinct from NCRPB) together with its public-private 'Utkrisht Society for Safe Haryana' vehicle -- a partnership chaired ex officio by the state DGP as chief patron, through which GMDA and Maruti Suzuki (as a CSR funder) have jointly rolled out an integrated traffic-management camera network (roughly 400 cameras across 23 Gurugram junctions) -- a genuinely distinct institutional wrinkle worth CrashFree India's attention beyond the standard PWD/Transport/Police triad, though it is a Haryana-created vehicle rather than a joint NCR-wide statutory body.

Underlying this political layer, India's constitutional Seventh Schedule splits road-related subjects across the Union and State Lists, and because roads, transport and police all sit substantially on the State List (with the Union retaining National Highways, the Motor Vehicles Act framework, and centrally sponsored schemes like PMGSY), Haryana's state government and its departments remain the primary point of leverage for almost all road-safety interventions CrashFree India will pursue in this state.

governance_bodies.name: Public Works Department (Buildings & Roads) [PWD B&R]
governance_bodies.mandate: Haryana's premier works department: planning, design, construction and maintenance of State Highways, Major District Roads, government buildings, and (per the department's own site structure) PMGSY rural roads directly, rather than via a separate rural-works department as in Bihar/Jharkhand/Karnataka/Tamil Nadu/Madhya Pradesh. Also constructs NH stretches not entrusted to NHAI. Source: haryanapwd.gov.in -- Home (https://haryanapwd.gov.in/); haryanapwd.gov.in -- PMGSY (https://haryanapwd.gov.in/home/PMGSY.html) [both cited from the prior research pass; this pass's re-fetch attempts on both URLs returned connection resets, so their content could not be independently re-verified today -- see Source Audit].
governance_bodies.roads_owned: State Highways (SH), Major District Roads (MDR), NH stretches not entrusted to NHAI, Other District Roads/Village Roads (rural roads, via PMGSY and the state's own rural-roads programmes), and government buildings statewide. Outside Gurugram and Faridabad's metropolitan-authority areas, PWD (B&R) is Haryana's dominant road-owning department for everything above the municipal level.
governance_bodies.hierarchy: Minister, PWD (B&R) -> Administrative Secretary (IAS) -> Engineer-in-Chief -> Chief Engineers (Wings) -> Superintending Engineers (Circles) -> Executive Engineers (Divisions) -> Sub-Divisional Officers. The department publishes its own detailed organisation charts down to Junior Engineer/Superintendent/HDM/ADM level, but this pass could not independently confirm the names of the current Engineer-in-Chief or Chief Engineers against an allowed, dated source -- a 2024-dated Haryana PWD Project Management Unit document and an outdated LinkedIn profile were the only leads found, both insufficient for a firm identification -- flagged as a research gap rather than asserted.
governance_bodies.subordinate_bodies: Haryana State Roads & Bridges Development Corporation Ltd (HSRDC) -- the department's dedicated BOT/BOOT/BOLT road-and-bridge-development corporation, registered office Panchkula (see separate entry). The PMGSY rural-roads function is administered through an implementing-agency structure headquartered inside the PWD (B&R) complex (Nirman Sadan, Sector 33-A, Chandigarh) with its own Executive Engineer (PMGSY); a prior pass found this agency referred to as the "Haryana Rural Roads and Infrastructure Development Agency" in a non-government-hosted document, and this specific name and legal/SRRDA status could not be re-confirmed against a directly-fetchable haryanapwd.gov.in or national PMGSY (pmgsy.nic.in) primary source in this pass, because haryanapwd.gov.in returned repeated connection resets in this pass -- flagged as an ongoing, unresolved gap.

Source: hsrdc.org.in -- About Us (https://hsrdc.org.in/AboutUS).
governance_bodies.roads_owned: Toll roads, expressways and major bridges developed on BOT/BOOT/BOLT terms; the state's dedicated vehicle for private/concession-financed road and bridge infrastructure, distinct from PWD (B&R)'s departmentally-executed SH/MDR network.
governance_bodies.hierarchy: A public limited company under the administrative control of the PWD (B&R) Department. Its own website lists a functioning Board of Directors, with 104 recorded BOD meetings as of this pass's fetch (agendas/minutes running from the 1st/2nd joint meeting through the 104th), but does not name a current Chairman or Managing Director on its public pages. Source: hsrdc.org.in -- Board of Directors Agenda (https://hsrdc.org.in/BODAgenda).
governance_bodies.subordinate_bodies: Not established from the sources reviewed in this pass.
governance_bodies.decision_making_power: Facilitates toll collection on developed roads and manages BOT/BOOT/BOLT project construction and maintenance per its own stated mandate.
governance_bodies.data_role: Not established from the sources reviewed in this pass.
governance_bodies.performance_issues: No named current Chairman/Managing Director could be confirmed via HSRDC's own website in this pass -- a governance-transparency gap relative to some other states' road corporations researched in this series, where leadership is named on the corporation's own site.
governance_bodies.meeting_frequency: 104 Board of Directors meetings recorded on the corporation's own website as of this pass, implying a regular, ongoing meeting cadence; the corresponding date range was not independently established.

governance_bodies.name: Gurugram Metropolitan Development Authority (GMDA)
governance_bodies.mandate: A dedicated, statutorily-created metropolitan planning and infrastructure authority for Gurugram specifically (established by the GMDA Act, 2017), distinct from the Town & Country Planning Department and from HSVP (the statewide urban-estate-development body covering the rest of Haryana). Source: tcpharyana.gov.in -- GMDA Act (https://tcpharyana.gov.in/Notification/GMDA%20Act.pdf).
governance_bodies.roads_owned: Gurugram metropolitan-level arterial road, master-drainage and mobility infrastructure planning/execution, coordinating in parallel with (and sometimes overlapping) PWD (B&R) on SH/NH-adjacent stretches and the Municipal Corporation of Gurugram (MCG) on internal municipal roads -- a three-way GMDA/PWD/MCG jurisdictional split specifically in Gurugram, on top of which NHAI and HSVP (as ROW facilitator) sit for NH/expressway works passing through the district.
governance_bodies.hierarchy: Chairman: Chief Minister of Haryana (ex officio, per the GMDA Act structure paralleled at HSVP -- see that entry). Maintains its own "Coordination Committee" bringing together GMDA, MCG, HSVP, PWD (B&R), Haryana Police and utility agencies. Source: gmda.gov.in -- Coordination Committee (https://gmda.gov.in/committee/coordination.html?language=en).
governance_bodies.subordinate_bodies: Not established from the sources reviewed in this pass.

governance_bodies.name: Haryana Shahari Vikas Pradhikaran (HSVP) [formerly HUDA]
governance_bodies.mandate: Statewide statutory urban-estate development authority for Haryana, responsible for planned development of residential/commercial sectors and their internal infrastructure (roads, water supply, sewerage, drainage) across the state EXCEPT Gurugram and Faridabad, where GMDA and the Faridabad Metropolitan Development Authority (FMDA) now hold the equivalent metropolitan-level role. HSVP also functions as the state's nodal right-of-way (ROW) agency handing over land to NHAI for national expressway projects passing through Haryana. Source: hsvphry.org.in (https://hsvphry.org.in/); The Tribune, 4 October 2021 ('HSVP is working as the nodal agency for providing right of way (ROW) to the NHAI for the expressway') (https://www.tribuneindia.com/news/haryana/make-upcoming-expressway-signal-free-in-faridabad-nhai-told-319920/amp).
governance_bodies.roads_owned: Sector/internal roads within HSVP-developed urban estates statewide (outside Gurugram/Faridabad), until formal handover to the relevant Municipal Corporation/Council -- a handover step that, per a widely-documented India-wide pattern seen in this research series (e.g. Bihar's Development-Authority-to-ULB handover gap), is frequently delayed, though no specific, current, audited Haryana instance was identified in this pass.
governance_bodies.hierarchy: Chairman: Chief Minister of Haryana, ex officio -> Chief Administrator, HSVP (IAS) -> Administrator, HSVP HQ -> district-level Estate Officers (an Estate Officer, HSVP/HUDA sits as a named member on every District Road Safety Committee in Haryana -- see that entry). Source: hsvphry.org.in -- Who's Who (https://hsvphry.org.in/Home/Whoswho).

governance_bodies.name: Urban Local Bodies (Municipal Corporations) and the emerging Faridabad Metropolitan Development Authority (FMDA)
governance_bodies.mandate: Municipal governance for major urban centres statewide, including internal municipal roads, footpaths, streetlights and drainage. Faridabad has, in addition, an emerging metropolitan-level authority (FMDA) paralleling GMDA, whose CEO post has at times been held jointly with the GMDA CEO's -- Faridabad's road-governance structure is consequently converging on Gurugram's multi-body pattern (Municipal Corporation / metropolitan authority / PWD), though FMDA's own legal basis and current independent operating status were not confirmed against a primary FMDA source in this pass (fmda.gov.in does not resolve, and faridabad.nic.in lists FMDA as a district department but with no populated official-directory data). Source: faridabad.nic.in -- Faridabad Metropolitan Development Authority (FMDA) directory listing (https://faridabad.nic.in/department/faridabad-metropolitan-development-authority-fmda/).
governance_bodies.roads_owned: Municipal Corporations of Gurugram (MCG), Faridabad (MCF), Panchkula, and others own/maintain municipal roads, footpaths, and drainage within their limits, separate from PWD (B&R)'s SH/MDR/NH remit and, in Gurugram's case, separate again from GMDA's metropolitan-level planning role -- a three-way (MC/GMDA-or-FMDA/PWD) jurisdictional split specifically in Gurugram and, increasingly, Faridabad.
governance_bodies.hierarchy: Minister, Urban Local Bodies -> Municipal Commissioners (IAS, per corporation) -> Ward Councillors. governance_bodies.name: State and District Road Safety Council/Committee
governance_bodies.mandate: Building awareness about road safety and traffic laws, and initiating steps to reduce road accidents, under Section 215 of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988, which empowers a State Government to constitute a State Road Safety Council and District Road Safety Committees by gazette notification. Haryana's version was notified by the Transport Department via a gazette notification dated 15 December 2017 (implementation reported from 8 January 2018). Source: Motor Vehicles Act 1988, Section 215 (https://indiankanoon.org/doc/33016598/); haryanatransport.gov.in -- State & District Road Safety Council & Committee notification, 15.12.2017 (https://haryanatransport.gov.in/sites/default/files/Notification_Instructions_Orders_Circulations/14.State&DistrictRoadSafetyCouncil&Committee15.12.2017.pdf) -- primary document identified but not directly fetchable in this pass (as in the prior pass); corroborated via The Statesman, 'Road safety council for each district in Haryana' (https://www.thestatesman.com/cities/road-safety-council-district-haryana-1502560372.html).
governance_bodies.roads_owned: Not applicable -- a coordinating/oversight body, not a road-owning one.
governance_bodies.hierarchy: State Road Safety Council: chaired by the Transport Minister, with the Administrative Secretaries of Home, School Education, Public Works (Buildings and Roads), Transport, and Health as members (source: haryanatransport.gov.in Road Safety Action Plan). District Road Safety Committees: one per district, chaired by the district Deputy Commissioner.
governance_bodies.subordinate_bodies: District Road Safety Committees, one per district.

governance_bodies.decision_making_power: District Road Safety Committee full composition (unusually detailed, and directly sourced): Superintendent of Police; Superintending Engineer (PWD); Chief Medical Officer; General Manager, Haryana Roadways; all Sub-Divisional Officers (Civil); District Education Officer and Elementary Education Officer; Estate Officer, Haryana Urban Development Authority (HSVP); municipal representatives; District Development and Panchayat Officer; Executive Engineer, Agricultural Marketing Board; NHAI Project Director; Divisional Forest Officer; superintending engineers of utility companies; and two non-government road safety experts, nominated by the chairman. telangana.political_context: A. Revanth Reddy (Congress) has served as Chief Minister of Telangana since 7 December 2023, heading the state's first Congress government since Telangana's 2014 creation. Cabinet portfolios were allocated shortly after, with the CM personally retaining Municipal Administration & Urban Development (MAUD), General Administration, and Law & Order (i.e., Home/Police), plus all unallocated portfolios -- meaning the same office controls both statewide enforcement and Hyderabad's urban civic administration (GHMC oversight sits under MAUD), a pattern also seen in Bihar, Jharkhand, Tamil Nadu, Assam, and Haryana. Mallu Bhatti Vikramarka serves as Deputy Chief Minister and Finance Minister, giving him direct control over the treasury account into which the new Road Safety Cess revenue flows; he presented the state Budget in March 2025 and continues in the role (Deccan Chronicle, South First, ANI). The full December 2023 cabinet portfolio list rests primarily on a single South First article, with Komatireddy Venkat Reddy (Roads and Buildings), Ponnam Prabhakar (Transport), and N. Uttam Kumar Reddy (Irrigation and CAD, Food and Civil Supplies) independently cross-checked. On the bureaucratic side, Sanjay Jaju, IAS (1992 batch) became Chief Secretary on 26 June 2026, succeeding K. Ramakrishna Rao, and is set to remain in service until February 2029 (Deccan Chronicle, The News Minute). C. V. Anand, IPS, took charge as Telangana DGP on 1 May 2026 -- moving from the bureaucratic-facing post of Special Chief Secretary (Home) -- and immediately announced plans for a dedicated Traffic Management and Road Safety Bureau. That bureau, TG-TMARS (Telangana Traffic Management, Road and Rail Safety Bureau), was formally created by Government Order on 24 September 2026 (one day before this research pass), to be led by an officer of Additional DGP/IG rank across four wings (Traffic Management, Road & Rail Safety, Administrative, and Vigilance & Standards); DGP Anand said the bureau would help address roughly 8,000 road deaths recorded in Telangana in the preceding year, but no director has yet been named in any source found. Six senior IPS officers, including Mahesh Bhagwat (who held the ADG Railways & Road Safety post in 2024 before moving to ADG/DGP-rank Law & Order) and V. C. Sajjanar, were promoted to DGP rank in April 2026 while remaining in their existing postings (Newsmeter, The Hans India). On road infrastructure, K. Ilambarithi, IAS, was named State Transport Commissioner effective 31 October 2025 (moving from Secretary, MA&UD), and was still active in that post chairing a transport-tax rationalisation meeting reported by Deccan Chronicle on 31 July 2026. R. V. Karnan, IAS, has been GHMC Commissioner since mid-2025 (the fourth commissioner in roughly ten months at that point) and remained in post through Ganesh Festival preparations in September 2026; he is on record (Telangana Today, 1 September 2025) stating over 90% of Greater Hyderabad's potholes had been repaired under a 'Road Safety Drive'. Sarfaraz Ahmad, IAS, has served as HMDA Metropolitan Commissioner since June 2024 and held the post as of the most recent independently corroborated reporting found (2025); his 2026 status could not be independently reconfirmed in this pass and should be checked before outreach. HYDRAA Commissioner AV Ranganath, IPS, remains in post as of this audit but under continuing litigation: a Telangana High Court single judge ordered his removal (27 July 2026, citing 63 contempt cases), a division bench stayed that order (1 September 2026), and the matter is listed for a further hearing on 3 November 2026; Advocate General A. Sudarshan Reddy personally represented the state/Ranganath's position in that litigation (Telangana Today). In the Assembly, the Telangana Legislative Assembly passed the Motor Vehicles Taxation (Amendment) Bill, 2025 on 2 January 2026, creating a one-time Road Safety Cess on new vehicle registrations effective 1 March 2026, expected to raise roughly Rs 300 crore annually for black-spot rectification, speed cameras, Automated Driving Testing Stations, and District Road Safety Committee strengthening; Transport Minister Ponnam Prabhakar personally tabled it, citing incidents such as the Vikarabad bus accident. Roads and Buildings Minister Komatireddy Venkat Reddy has separately and repeatedly (2024 through 2026) named specific black-spot locations for remediation (e.g., 17 sites on the Hyderabad-Vijayawada highway; Choutuppal and Chityal) and has allocated Rs 500 crore toward flyovers/bridges at accident-prone black spots. On the opposition benches, K. Chandrashekar Rao (KCR), BRS, remains the formally recognised Leader of Opposition (since 16 December 2023) but has drawn sustained Congress criticism in 2026 for near-total Assembly non-attendance (Congress alleged just 3 days of attendance over roughly 1,000 days, per a September 2026 protest); his son K. T. Rama Rao (KTR) is BRS's more publicly active Working President and the more realistic opposition point of contact. At the city-police operational level, Joint CP (Traffic) Hyderabad D. Joel Davis, IPS, has built a genuinely data-driven, recurring road-safety profile across 2026 -- publishing accident and child-casualty statistics, school-zone infrastructure-gap surveys (school-zone signage, speed-limit signage, zebra crossings), and enforcement drives -- making him one of the most concretely engaged road-safety officials identified for Telangana in this pass.

maharashtra.political_context: Maharashtra is governed by the Mahayuti coalition (BJP + Shiv Sena-Shinde + NCP-Ajit Pawar faction) formed after the November 2024 state assembly election. Devendra Fadnavis (BJP) became Chief Minister for a third time on 5 December 2024. On 28 January 2026, Deputy CM Ajit Pawar (NCP), who held Finance, Planning, State Excise and other portfolios, died along with four others when the Learjet 45 charter aircraft carrying him to Baramati crashed on approach in low visibility (confirmed via India's official news service and independently by Reuters wire coverage). Finance and Planning passed to CM Fadnavis the same week, and NCP's Legislature Party unanimously chose Pawar's widow, Sunetra Pawar (sitting Rajya Sabha MP), as his successor; she was sworn in as Deputy CM on 31 January 2026, becoming Maharashtra's first woman Deputy CM, and was allotted State Excise, Sports & Youth Welfare, and Minority Development & Aukaf -- not Finance or Planning. Multiple Jan-Feb 2026 reports indicated NCP intended to press for Finance/Planning to be handed to the party after the 2026-27 budget session (which began 23 February 2026); this research pass could not independently confirm whether that handover has actually occurred by September 2026, so Fadnavis should be treated as the last-confirmed holder of Finance & Planning pending fresh verification (flagged). Deputy CM Eknath Shinde (Shiv Sena) continues to hold Urban Development, Housing, and Public Works (including Public Undertakings), and is ex officio Chairman of both the MMRDA Authority and MSRDC by virtue of the Urban Development portfolio. PWD itself remains split between a 'Public Works (excluding Public Undertakings)' wing held by a dedicated PWD minister (Shivendrasinhraje Bhosale) and a 'Public Works (including Public Undertakings)' wing nominally under Shinde -- a jurisdictional split distinctive to Maharashtra among the states researched so far. CM Fadnavis is widely reported to personally direct the Home Department and state police (a July 2026 government press item shows him directly instructing the Home Department and police on enforcement matters), consistent with the established pattern of the CM retaining Home. The Chief Secretary is Rajesh Aggarwal (in post since 1 December 2025, reconfirmed current via an 18 March 2026 Raj Bhavan record of him meeting the Governor). On the road-safety governance front, the single most significant development this pass is that Maharashtra's statutory State Road Safety Council -- dormant since 3 April 2023 -- finally reconvened on 23 September 2026 (its 13th meeting, 1,267 days after the 12th), with Transport Minister Pratap Sarnaik directing coordinated action across police, PWD and health departments amid 1,17,070 accidents and 50,488 deaths recorded statewide since the Council's last sitting. Sarnaik's ministry also announced a slate of initiatives the same week: a digital 108/private ambulance integration platform, mandatory road-safety audits with 10% of the PWD budget earmarked for safety, trauma-centre expansion, a PM-RAHAT cashless-treatment rollout, and an 11-district 'Zero Fatality District' programme, alongside a reported 6% year-on-year decline in fatalities for Jan-Jul 2026 vs the same 2025 period. Separately, Transport Commissioner Vivek Bhimanwar's office issued a 11 February 2026 circular declaring 2026 the 'Save Two-Wheeler Riders & Pedestrians Year' following a state-level review (two-wheeler riders were 57% of 2025's 15,549 road deaths, pedestrians 21%). On the opposition side, the formal post of Leader of the Opposition in the Legislative Assembly has been vacant since 23 November 2024 because no single opposition party crossed the 10%-of-seats threshold after the 2024 rout of the Maha Vikas Aghadi bloc; Congress's Vijay Wadettiwar functions as the de facto senior opposition voice as Congress Legislature Party leader (a status distinct from the vacant formal LoP title) and has repeatedly criticised the government on infrastructure and fund-allocation issues, including the Mumbai-Pune Expressway 'Missing Link' closure. The opposition's position weakened further in June 2026 when six of Shiv Sena (UBT)'s seven Lok Sabha MPs defected to merge with CM ally Eknath Shinde's Shiv Sena, cementing the Mahayuti's dominance and reducing Uddhav Thackeray's parliamentary strength to three MPs -- a realignment that also reduces the number of distinct opposition channels CrashFree India can engage for cross-party road-safety advocacy. Given India's Seventh Schedule division of subjects, roads, transport and police sit substantially on the State List, making Maharashtra's state government and its departments (rather than the Union) the primary point of leverage for most road-safety interventions, with the Union mattering mainly for National Highway stretches, the Motor Vehicles Act framework, and centrally sponsored schemes.

governance_bodies.name: Public Works Department (PWD), Government of Maharashtra
governance_bodies.mandate: Construction, widening and maintenance of State Highways (SH) and Major District Roads (MDR); public buildings, government residential complexes, and irrigation-adjacent civil works. Maharashtra's PWD is administratively split into two ministerial charges -- 'Public Works (excluding Public Undertakings)' and 'Public Works (including Public Undertakings)' -- with the latter tied to the MSRDC-linked corporate/PPP works portfolio; both sit under the same departmental secretariat for civil-service purposes.

governance_bodies.hierarchy: Additional Chief Secretary, PWD -> Secretary (Roads) and Secretary (Works) as parallel secretarial charges -> Chief Engineers (region/zone-wise, e.g. Mumbai, Pune, Nashik, Nagpur, Amravati, Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar zones) -> Superintending Engineers (Circles) -> Executive Engineers (Divisions) -> Sub-Divisional/Assistant Engineers in the field, per the department's own site.

governance_bodies.name: Maharashtra Road Safety Fund (RSF)
governance_bodies.mandate: A dedicated cess-funded corpus for road-safety measures, established via a Road Safety Cess levied on vehicle registrations since 24 October 2016 (0.5%-10% of one-time/annual tax, collected once per vehicle's lifetime, varying by vehicle type).
governance_bodies.roads_owned: Not road-specific -- a cross-cutting safety-equipment/campaign fund rather than an infrastructure owner.
governance_bodies.hierarchy: A seven-member high-power committee chaired by the Chief Secretary approves proposals; a Personal Ledger Account (PLA), established 9 February 2017, allows the corpus to roll over annually without lapsing.
governance_bodies.subordinate_bodies: None -- a funding mechanism, not an implementing body; funds are disbursed to the Transport Department, Highway Police, and MSRDC.

The 23 Sept 2026 Council meeting's new directive that PWD earmark 10% of its own funds for safety works suggests the state is diversifying funding routes rather than relying solely on RSF disbursement.

governance_bodies.name: State Road Safety Council (SRSC)
governance_bodies.mandate: Statutory road-safety coordination body constituted under Section 215 of the Motor Vehicles Act 1988 (operationalised via Rule 215 of the Central Motor Vehicles Rules), established May 2015; required to meet at least twice a year (biannually) under the Rules.
governance_bodies.roads_owned: Not an implementing body -- a review/coordination council.
governance_bodies.hierarchy: Chaired by the Transport Minister (Pratap Sarnaik); Transport Commissioner serves as member-secretary. 22-member body including state officials from Home, Transport, PWD, Health and BMC, plus special invitees from public health, urban development and media.
governance_bodies.subordinate_bodies: District Road Safety Committees (DRSCs) at district level.
