governance_bodies.decision_making_power: Reviews accident trends, identifies dangerous locations, monitors safety measures, and coordinates inter-departmental action. At its 23 September 2026 meeting (the 13th since inception), the Council: directed Transport, Police, PWD and Health departments to coordinate; mandated PWD earmark 10% of funds for road-safety works and conduct safety audits at all project stages; proposed bringing 108 and private ambulances onto a single digital dispatch platform; proposed an air-ambulance policy for expressways (incl. Samruddhi), coastal routes and remote areas; proposed trauma-care centres within every 50 km; proposed electronic weigh-in-motion systems for overloaded vehicles and remote-sensing emissions checks; and extended the 'Zero Fatality District' data-driven programme to 11 districts.
governance_bodies.data_role: Reviews aggregate state crash-fatality data (1,17,070 accidents and 50,488 deaths, April 2023-June 2026, per the Council's own September 2026 figures) rather than operating a data system itself.
governance_bodies.performance_issues: MAJOR UPDATE this pass (resolving the prior file's single largest documented governance gap): the Council FINALLY MET on 23 September 2026 -- its 13th meeting, held 1,267 days (roughly 41.6 months) after the previous meeting on 3 April 2023, despite the mandatory biannual-meeting requirement under the Central Motor Vehicles Rules. Sarnaik assumed the Transport portfolio on 24 December 2024, meaning the meeting followed roughly 638 days into his own tenure. This closes the specific 'has the Council met since April 2023' research question that the prior verification pass left open (it had only confirmed a promised 'first week of July 2026' meeting that could not itself be verified as having occurred) -- the Council met roughly 11 weeks later than that promise, in late September rather than early July 2026.
governance_bodies.meeting_frequency: Biannual meetings are mandatory by regulation; only 13 have been held since the Council's 2015 inception as of the 23 September 2026 meeting, an average far below the mandated cadence.

governance_bodies.name: District Road Safety Committees (DRSCs), Maharashtra
governance_bodies.mandate: Constituted under Section 215(3) of the Motor Vehicles Act 1988, which empowers a State Government to constitute a District Road Safety Committee for each district by Gazette notification, consisting of a Chairman and such other members as the Government considers necessary.
governance_bodies.roads_owned: None (coordination body).
governance_bodies.hierarchy: The Supreme Court Committee on Road Safety (SCCoRS) has directed a uniform national template for DRSC composition -- District Collector/Magistrate as Chairman, with the Superintendent of Police/DCP, Chief Medical Officer of Health, an Executive Engineer (PWD-Roads), a MoRTH regional representative, an NHAI Project Director, a ULB Executive Officer, and at least one civil-society/NGO representative as Members -- via a directive circulated to all states.
governance_bodies.subordinate_bodies: None specified beyond membership.
governance_bodies.decision_making_power: Required to meet regularly to track district crash data, identify local black spots, coordinate multi-department road-safety action, and feed district-level findings up to the State Road Safety Council; specific Maharashtra-wide compliance data on meeting frequency was not independently confirmed in this pass.
governance_bodies.data_role: District-level crash and black-spot data aggregation feeding into the State Road Safety Council's statewide statistics (e.g. the 1,17,070-accident/50,488-death figure cited at the September 2026 state Council meeting is necessarily built from district-level reporting).
governance_bodies.performance_issues: Maharashtra's specific district-by-district DRSC notification (composition, and whether it has been updated to the SCCoRS's post-2022 uniform template) could not be independently located or confirmed in this pass -- flagged as a research gap. Given that the State Road Safety Council itself went 1,267 days without meeting, and DRSCs are meant to feed the state Council, a genuine question -- not resolved in this pass -- is whether Maharashtra's DRSCs remained active as a reporting channel during that gap or lapsed alongside it.
governance_bodies.meeting_frequency: Not independently confirmed for Maharashtra specifically in this pass; the national SCCoRS template envisages regular (commonly monthly, per other states' notified rules) district-level meetings.

governance_bodies.name: Brihanmumbai Municipal Corporation (BMC / MCGM)
governance_bodies.mandate: Municipal governance for Greater Mumbai, including construction, maintenance and safety of the city's municipal road network, drains, and civic infrastructure -- one of India's richest civic bodies by budget.
governance_bodies.roads_owned: Approximately 1,950 km of the roughly 2,000 km of roads within Greater Mumbai are BMC-maintained municipal roads (the remaining c. 50 km being State Highway stretches under PWD), per BMC's own City Development Plan documentation. Since 2022, BMC has also taken over maintenance of the Eastern Express Highway (EEH) and Western Express Highway (WEH) from MMRDA (which had itself taken these over earlier from the state PWD) -- illustrating how a single Mumbai corridor's custodianship can shift between PWD, MMRDA and BMC over time. BMC additionally owns and built the c. 29 km Mumbai Coastal Road (Marine Drive to the northern suburbs), an 8-lane project combining reclaimed-land roads, sea-facing stilted sections and a twin undersea tunnel under Malabar Hill.
governance_bodies.hierarchy: An elected wing (Mayor, when the corporation is in session -- note that BMC has operated for extended periods under an Administrator/Municipal Commissioner in the absence of an elected general body since 2022, pending corporation elections) and a separate administrative wing headed by the Municipal Commissioner, an IAS officer appointed by the state government (not answerable to an elected Mayor for personnel matters); Additional Municipal Commissioners and a Chief Engineer (Roads & Traffic) sit below the Commissioner for road-specific functions.
governance_bodies.subordinate_bodies: City Engineer's department (Roads & Traffic); ward-level Assistant Engineers for local road maintenance and complaint resolution.

governance_bodies.meeting_frequency: Not established from the sources reviewed for this pass; BMC has operated without an elected general body/Standing Committee since 2022 pending corporation elections, per contemporaneous reporting on the 2026 BMC election cycle -- meaning committee-level oversight of road works has, for an extended period, run through the Administrator/Commissioner rather than an elected Standing Committee.

governance_bodies.roads_owned: Major MMR-wide connector infrastructure including the Mumbai Trans Harbour Link (Atal Bihari Vajpayee Sewri-Nhava Sheva Atal Setu, owned and implemented by MMRDA per a 4 February 2009 state government decision), the Eastern Freeway, and the Santacruz-Chembur Link Road (SCLR) -- distinct from BMC's ordinary city-street network and from MSRDC's tolled expressways/sea links.
governance_bodies.hierarchy: The MMRDA Authority is chaired ex officio by the Minister for Urban Development (Deputy CM Eknath Shinde); day-to-day executive administration is led by the Metropolitan Commissioner, an IAS officer.
governance_bodies.subordinate_bodies: MMRDA's own Engineering Division executes/maintains its road and connector projects.

governance_bodies.name: Rural Development & Panchayat Raj Department / Maharashtra Rural Road Development Association (MRRDA) / Zilla Parishad Works Departments
governance_bodies.mandate: Rural road connectivity and rural infrastructure. The Rural Development & Panchayat Raj Department sets policy and runs the Pradhan Mantri Gram Sadak Yojana (PMGSY) scheme page for Maharashtra; the Maharashtra Rural Road Development Association (MRRDA) is the state's dedicated executing agency for PMGSY and the state-funded Mukhya Mantri Gram Sadak Yojana (MMGSY)-equivalent programmes, coordinating through regional offices and Project Implementation Units (PIUs); day-to-day rural road works and buildings within each district are additionally executed through that district's Zilla Parishad Works Department (Bandhkam Vibhag).
governance_bodies.roads_owned: Rural roads (Other District Roads/ODR and Village Roads/VR equivalent categories) connecting villages, executed via MRRDA (PMGSY-funded works) or the district Zilla Parishad's own Works Department (locally funded/maintained roads and buildings).
governance_bodies.hierarchy: Minister, Rural Development & Panchayat Raj -> Department Secretariat (policy, scheme administration) -> MRRDA (a semi-autonomous executing agency with a Project Management Unit overseeing six regional offices and PIUs) running in parallel with each district's Zilla Parishad Works Department, which reports up its own ZP administrative line (CEO, Zilla Parishad) rather than to MRRDA directly.
governance_bodies.subordinate_bodies: MRRDA regional offices and PIUs; district Zilla Parishad Works Departments (e.g. Zilla Parishad Thane and Zilla Parishad Nagpur each maintain a dedicated 'Works Department' page describing construction/maintenance/repair of roads and buildings under ZP jurisdiction).

governance_bodies.name: Public Health Department -- Maharashtra Emergency Medical Services (MEMS) & Trauma Care
governance_bodies.mandate: Institutional home for pre-hospital emergency response and trauma care, operating the Maharashtra Emergency Medical Services (MEMS) '108' free ambulance programme statewide.
governance_bodies.roads_owned: None (health/trauma-care role, not road ownership).
governance_bodies.hierarchy: Minister, Public Health -> Public Health Department secretariat -> MEMS programme management (a state-run/PPP-supported ambulance dispatch and operations structure) -> district Civil Surgeons for hospital-side trauma-centre coordination.
governance_bodies.subordinate_bodies: MEMS ambulance fleet -- 937 ambulances deployed phase-wise statewide (233 Advanced Life Support/ALS and 704 Basic Life Support/BLS units), per the Public Health Department's own scheme page.
governance_bodies.decision_making_power: Runs the 108 toll-free, 24x7, free-of-cost ambulance dispatch system on a 'Golden Hour' response strategy (patient to nearest hospital within the first hour); trauma/injury cases account for 13.32% of all 108 call reasons statewide, per the department's own published utilisation data. At the 23 September 2026 State Road Safety Council meeting, the Health Department was directed to help bring 108 and private ambulances onto a single digital dispatch platform, to support an air-ambulance policy for expressways/coastal routes/remote areas, to support trauma-care centres within every 50 km, and to implement the PM-RAHAT scheme for cashless treatment up to Rs 1.5 lakh for road-accident victims.
governance_bodies.data_role: One of the core stakeholder departments feeding hospital-side/trauma data into any future integrated crash database; specific iRAD/e-DAR integration for Maharashtra not independently confirmed in the sources reviewed for this pass.
governance_bodies.performance_issues: MEMS's stated ambulance fleet (937 units) relative to Maharashtra's population and geography, and the state's actual average ambulance response time, were not independently benchmarked against a 'Golden Hour'/10-minute national standard in the sources reviewed for this pass -- flagged as a research gap analogous to the documented response-time gaps found in other states' MEMS-equivalent services.
governance_bodies.meeting_frequency: Not established from the sources reviewed for this pass; participates in the State Road Safety Council's coordination cadence.

governance_bodies.roads_owned: None.
governance_bodies.hierarchy: The Authority is chaired ex officio by the Chief Minister (per the Disaster Management Act 2005's standard state-authority structure, with the Chief Secretary as CEO); day-to-day departmental administration runs through a dedicated Minister for Disaster Management/Relief & Rehabilitation.
governance_bodies.subordinate_bodies: State Emergency Operations Centre; coordination links to the National Disaster Response Force (NDRF), IMD, INCOIS and CWC for early warning.

maharashtra.source_audit: This pass rebuilt Maharashtra's governance_bodies, road_ownership_matrix, road_lifecycle, district_level_actors, quick_reference_matrix and funding_architecture sections from scratch, applying CrashFree India's source-tier policy strictly: allowed sources used were (a) official government sources -- pwd.maharashtra.gov.in, transport.maharashtra.gov.in, mahapolice.gov.in, mumbaipolice.gov.in, highwaypolice.maharashtra.gov.in, mmrda.maharashtra.gov.in, sdma.maharashtra.gov.in, rajbhavan-maharashtra.gov.in, msrdc.in (a wholly state-government-owned corporation's own official site), and zpthane.maharashtra.gov.in/zpnagpur.maharashtra.gov.in for Zilla Parishad structure; (b)/(c) mainstream Indian press with clear bylines -- Free Press Journal, The Quint, Tribune India, Nagpur Today, and newsdrum.in -- used where no equivalent government source was locatable (e.g. the State Road Safety Council's meeting history and the 23 September 2026 meeting's specific directives, which are reported but not yet published as a government notification/minutes document as of this pass). No Wikipedia, social-media or unsourced-blog citations were used anywhere in these six sections; every citation carries a real, working URL. The single most significant finding of this pass is that Maharashtra's State Road Safety Council -- documented in the prior pass as inactive since 3 April 2023, with an unconfirmed promise of a 'first week of July 2026' revival meeting -- in fact met on 23 September 2026 (its 13th meeting, 1,267 days after the 12th), per Free Press Journal's same-week coverage; this closes what had been flagged as the state's single largest documented road-safety-governance failure, while opening a new, immediate-term question (whether the meeting's specific commitments are implemented) that could not be assessed given the two-day gap between that meeting and this pass's reference date. A number of named office-holders carried over from the prior pass's Wikipedia-sourced key_positions entries (Chief Secretary Rajesh Aggarwal's personal RSF chairmanship; the DGP and Mumbai CP's identities) were independently re-verified in this pass against each office's own official government website rather than Wikipedia, and are now sourced accordingly. One office-holder claim from the prior pass (State Transport Commissioner Vivek Bhimanwar) was found, via an official Raj Bhavan Maharashtra notice, to be stale -- he was sworn in as MPSC Chairman on 18 February 2026 -- and his successor's name could not be confirmed in this pass; per the sourcing policy's 'omit anything that cannot be referenced' rule, no successor's name is asserted, and this is carried instead as an explicit research gap. This pass's WebSearch quota was exhausted before every open question (e.g. the current PWD Engineer-in-Chief, the current NHAI Regional Officer for Maharashtra, and Maharashtra's district-specific Road Safety Committee notification) could be independently resolved; these are disclosed as genuine, budget-limited gaps in the research_gaps array rather than silently omitted or guessed at. Several official Maharashtra government domains (msrdc.in, mmrda.maharashtra.gov.in, sdma.maharashtra.gov.in, pwd.maharashtra.gov.in, transport.maharashtra.gov.in) intermittently returned HTTP 503 errors on direct re-fetch during this pass; where a fact from one of these domains could not be re-fetched directly but had already surfaced in a dated, 2026-specific search-engine snippet drawn from that same official domain (e.g. MMRDA's Metropolitan Commissioner), it was retained with a note of the transient fetch failure rather than discarded, since the underlying evidence (the domain, the URL, and the dated official content) remained intact.
research_gaps: The current State Transport Commissioner's name is unresolved: Vivek L. Bhimanwar (the previously documented holder) was sworn in as Chairman of the Maharashtra Public Service Commission on 18 February 2026 per an official Raj Bhavan Maharashtra notice, but no successor's name as Transport Commissioner could be independently confirmed before this pass's search budget was exhausted. This should be directly confirmed with the Transport Department before any outreach material names the office-holder.
The Engineer-in-Chief, PWD (a position distinct from the Additional Chief Secretary and the two parallel Secretary posts identified in this pass) was not named in the sources reviewed for this pass.

NHAI's specific Regional Officer(s) for Maharashtra (the state is served by at least a Mumbai/Navi Mumbai regional office) were not named in the sources reviewed for this pass; only the office's physical address was confirmed.

Maharashtra's District Road Safety Committee-specific Gazette notification (composition, and whether it follows the Supreme Court Committee on Road Safety's post-2022 uniform national template) could not be independently located in this pass -- a genuine gap given that the analogous notification was locatable for Bihar in a separate research pass.

Whether Maharashtra's District Road Safety Committees continued to function as a reporting channel during the State Road Safety Council's 1,267-day (April 2023-September 2026) inter-meeting gap, or whether district-level coordination lapsed alongside the state-level Council, is unresolved and is a strong candidate for direct field verification by CrashFree India.

Whether the specific commitments made at the 23 September 2026 State Road Safety Council meeting (single-platform ambulance dispatch, air-ambulance policy, trauma centres every 50 km, electronic weigh-in-motion systems, PWD's 10%-safety-fund earmark) are actually implemented, and on what timeline, could not be assessed in this pass since the meeting occurred only two days before this research pass's reference date (25 September 2026) -- a natural follow-up checkpoint for CrashFree India in early-to-mid 2027.

The precise division of rural-road responsibility between MRRDA (PMGSY-funded works) and each district's own Zilla Parishad Works Department for non-PMGSY rural roads was not fully resolved -- specifically, whether Maharashtra has a state-funded rural-road scheme directly analogous to other states' Mukhya Mantri Gram Sadak Yojana-type programmes, and if so, which agency executes it, is unconfirmed.

MSDMA's own road-safety-specific programming (as opposed to its general natural-hazard mandate) was not documented on the Authority's own website in this pass; its road-safety relevance to CrashFree India's work is inferred rather than directly evidenced, and is a candidate for direct follow-up with the Authority.

Maharashtra Emergency Medical Services (MEMS)'s actual average ambulance response time was not independently confirmed against the 'Golden Hour' standard the programme cites -- unlike some other states' MEMS-equivalent services, where a documented response-time gap (e.g. national 10-minute standard vs. an actual multi-times-longer average) was found in this multi-state research programme.

No Section A (recurring, personally-engaged road-safety champion) individual was independently identified for Maharashtra in this pass, echoing the prior pass's finding; worth checking directly with civil-society groups (e.g. SaveLIFE Foundation's Maharashtra-specific engagement) or IIT Bombay road-safety research groups, neither of which surfaced concretely in the sources reviewed.

gujarat.political_context: Bhupendra Patel (BJP) has been Chief Minister of Gujarat since 13 September 2021, re-elected for a second term on 12 December 2022. Unusually compared to other states researched, CM Patel personally holds the roads-engineering portfolio himself — General Administration, Administrative Reforms & Training, Planning, and Roads and Buildings and Capital Projects — publicly announcing large project allocations under his own name (e.g., ₹7,737 crore for 124 projects, October 2025) rather than delegating roads/PWD to a separate minister. Deputy CM Harsh Sanghavi (BJP), Deputy CM since 17 October 2025, holds Home Affairs, Law and Justice, Tourism, Industries, MSME & Civil Aviation, plus (continuing from his earlier appointment of 16 September 2021) Transport, Sports/Youth Affairs/Cultural Activities, Excise & Prohibition, and Border Security & Prisons — uniquely combining Home (police) and Transport, the two levers most directly relevant to enforcement and vehicle regulation, in one office. Other road-relevant ministers include Kanubhai Desai (Finance, Urban Development, Urban Housing) and Kunvarjibhai Bavaliya (Labour, Skill Development & Employment, Rural Development). governance_bodies.name: Gujarat Road Safety Authority (GRSA)
governance_bodies.mandate: A dedicated statutory Authority — the most institutionally developed road-safety-specific body found across all nine states researched to date alongside Karnataka's KSRSA. Established under the Gujarat Road Safety Authority Act, 2018, operating under the Gujarat Road Safety Rules and Orders, 2020. Implements road safety across four pillars: enforcement, road engineering, emergency care, and education.
governance_bodies.roads_owned: Not a road-owning body — a coordinating/implementing safety authority operating across road types.
governance_bodies.hierarchy: Chief Road Safety Commissioner at the operational head — per Section 3(4) of the Gujarat Road Safety Authority Act, 2018, this statutory post is "the Chief Executive Officer of the Authority" and "head of the staff of the Authority" — supported by a Joint Commissioner and Chief Enforcement Officer. The Authority itself has 14 statutory members drawn from Transport, Home, Health, Education, R&B, law enforcement, transport corporations, municipal administration, highway authorities, automobile associations, and two nominated road-safety experts. An Executive Committee, chaired by the Additional Chief Secretary (Transport), meets bimonthly. The broader Authority and a State Road Safety Council operate under the chairmanship of the Transport Minister (currently Deputy CM Harsh Sanghavi, by virtue of his Transport portfolio), meeting biannually. Re-verified 11 Sept 2026: statutory title corrected from "Road Safety Commissioner" to "Chief Road Safety Commissioner" per the Act text itself, upgrading the earlier single-secondary-source characterization.

uttar_pradesh.political_context: Yogi Adityanath (BJP) has been Chief Minister of Uttar Pradesh since 19 March 2017, now in his second term following the 2022 election, and remained CM through the state's constitutional Seventh Schedule-driven governance structure at least as recently as 25 September 2026, confirmed via a same-day report of his attendance at the Uttar Pradesh International Trade Show (UPITS-2026) inauguration. His personal portfolio concentration remains the single most extensive found across states researched to date: he directly holds Home, Public Works Department (PWD, Cabinet-rank charge vacant since June 2024), Law, General Administration, Cabinet Affairs, Information & Public Relations, Housing, Revenue, Mining & Geology, Institutional Finance, Planning, Civil Aviation, Food Safety & Drug Administration and other unallotted departments -- 25+ departments overall (Verified, The Print). PWD's Cabinet-rank charge history: Keshav Prasad Maurya (now Deputy CM) held it 19 March 2017 - 25 March 2022, succeeded by Cabinet Minister Jitin Prasada (25 March 2022 - 11 June 2024), who resigned on becoming a Union Minister of State; no Cabinet-rank successor has been appointed since. Minister of State Brijesh Singh (BJP MLA, Deoband) has held the PWD MoS portfolio continuously since 25 March 2022 and is the closest thing to a day-to-day ministerial face for PWD, though independent 2026-dated confirmation of his continuation was limited to lower-tier regional outlets (see flags). The two Deputy CMs -- Keshav Prasad Maurya (Rural Development since 25 March 2022; Food Processing Industries since 19 March 2017) and Brajesh Pathak (Health & Family Welfare, Medical Education since 25 March 2022) -- were reconfirmed in place through the UP cabinet's second expansion on 10 May 2026 (six new ministers inducted, taking the ministry to the constitutional ceiling of 60), a reshuffle that added Bhupendra Chaudhary and Manoj Pandey as Cabinet Ministers and four MLAs as Ministers of State without altering the Transport, PWD or Deputy CM portfolios. The Transport Minister is Daya Shankar Singh, Minister of State (Independent Charge) since 25 March 2022, reconfirmed still in post as recently as 23 September 2026 (Free Press Journal) and notable among all UP political figures for the most consistent, dated, road-safety-specific track record found in this pass -- spanning a December 2025 CM-chaired road-safety review, the January 2026 statewide 'Road Safety Month', and an April 2026 PPP-based bus-station-safety modernisation programme. Chief Secretary Shashi Prakash Goyal (1989-batch IAS, UP cadre) took charge on 1 August 2025, succeeding Manoj Kumar Singh, and is slated to serve until his own retirement in January 2027; no successor or 2026 transfer was found in this pass (absence-of-contradiction only). Rajeev Krishna (1991-batch IPS) was confirmed as UP's first permanent DGP since 2022 on 31 May 2026, ending an extended acting period, and remained active in the role as of 21 September 2026 (Indian Masterminds, addressing new recruits). Below the political layer, a September 2025 IPS reshuffle installed A. Satish Ganesh (1996-batch IPS) as ADG, Traffic & Road Safety Directorate, and he remained in that post and publicly engaged on road-safety technology as of August 2026 (Safe City & Intelligent Mobility India Summit). A parallel September 2025 IAS reshuffle resolved a standing research gap from the prior file: Deepak Kumar, IAS, was named Infrastructure & Industrial Development Commissioner (IIDC) and concurrently CEO of the Uttar Pradesh Expressways Industrial Development Authority (UPEIDA) -- the body that builds and operates UP's high-speed expressway network (Purvanchal, Bundelkhand, Ganga, Agra-Lucknow) where a large share of the state's highest-severity crashes occur -- resolving the prior file's 'UPEIDA CEO unconfirmed' flag. In a further structural shift reported in mid-2026, UPEIDA itself was moved out of the Industrial Development Minister's (Nand Gopal Gupta's) nominal oversight and placed directly under the Chief Minister's Infrastructure Development Department (The Print), meaning expressway safety and construction-quality accountability now runs more directly through the CM's office and IIDC Deepak Kumar than through the Industries portfolio. On the bureaucratic side, Sanjay Prasad (1995-batch IAS) was promoted to Additional Chief Secretary, Home & Confidential in January 2026, making him the senior-most bureaucrat under the CM's own Home portfolio and therefore a central node for traffic-enforcement policy and budget. On the opposition side, Mata Prasad Pandey (Samajwadi Party) has been Leader of the Opposition in the UP Legislative Assembly since 28 July 2024 (PRS Legislative Research), though no road-safety-specific statement by him was found in this pass; Samajwadi Party national president and former CM Akhilesh Yadav has instead been the most visible and recurring critical voice on road/expressway safety, most recently in a 17 September 2026 statement (The Print) alleging systemic construction-quality failures across the Purvanchal, Bundelkhand and Ganga Expressways. Separately, Congress Legislature Party leader Aradhana Mishra 'Mona' delivered a detailed, data-heavy road-safety intervention in the UP Assembly on 13 February 2026 (IANS), citing ~45,000 annual accidents and over 24,000 deaths and demanding engineering audits of black spots, statewide ITMS rollout and a traffic-police staffing fix (state has roughly 9,000 traffic personnel against an estimated requirement of 30,000, per her own figures as reported). As in the other pilot states, India's constitutional Seventh Schedule splits road-related subjects across the Union and State Lists, and because roads, transport and police sit substantially on the State List, Uttar Pradesh's state government and its departments -- not the Union -- are the primary point of leverage for almost all road-safety interventions CrashFree India will pursue in the state, with the Union mattering mainly for National Highway stretches, PMGSY funding rules and the Motor Vehicles Act framework.

governance_bodies.name: Public Works Department (PWD), Government of Uttar Pradesh
governance_bodies.mandate: The state's premier works department: construction, improvement, strengthening and maintenance of State Highways (SH) and Major District Roads (MDR), plus bridges, flyovers and rail-over-bridges (ROBs); also runs a dedicated Road Safety and IDS (road information/data system) programme area under its own portal.
governance_bodies.roads_owned: State Highways (SH), Major District Roads (MDR), and (via a National Highways wing, by the standard pattern used in most large states) NH stretches not yet entrusted to NHAI; road-safety-specific black-spot remediation across major cities (Varanasi, Lucknow, Kanpur, Meerut, and others) is run through PWD's own Road Safety programme.
governance_bodies.hierarchy: Cabinet-rank charge: vacant/held by CM Yogi Adityanath since Jitin Prasada's June 2024 exit; Minister of State: Brijesh Singh (since 25 Mar 2022, incumbent) -> Secretary, PWD -> Engineer-in-Chief (E-in-C, Head of Department) -> Chief Engineers by wing (Civil; Electrical/Mechanical) -> Superintending Engineers (Circles) -> Executive Engineers (Divisions) -> Assistant Engineers/field staff. UP PWD's own website lists a named Engineer-in-Chief and separate Chief Engineer (Civil) and Chief Engineer (Electrical/Mechanical) posts, confirming this Wing structure exists, though this pass could not reliably extract the current named officeholders from the site (persistent server errors on repeated attempts).
governance_bodies.subordinate_bodies: UPEIDA (a separate statutory authority for expressways, institutionally distinct from PWD proper) is not a PWD subordinate; no dedicated bridge-construction public-sector corporation analogous to Bihar's BRPNNL was identified for UP in this pass -- bridge works on SH/MDR/NH-with-PWD appear to be executed departmentally.

governance_bodies.name: Transport Department, Government of Uttar Pradesh
governance_bodies.mandate: A regulatory department implementing the Motor Vehicles Act 1988, Central Motor Vehicle Rules 1989, and State Taxation Acts, regulating road transport, passenger/freight movement, and public bus transport (via UPSRTC); also administers the UP Road Safety Fund Rules 2014 jointly with Police and Finance.
governance_bodies.roads_owned: None directly (regulatory, not road-owning); road-related functions: vehicle registration (VAHAN), driving licences (SARATHI), permits, vehicle fitness, road tax, enforcement policy coordination, and public bus transport via Uttar Pradesh State Road Transport Corporation (UPSRTC).
governance_bodies.hierarchy: Minister of State (Independent Charge): Daya Shankar Singh -> Additional Chief Secretary, Transport -> Transport Commissioner -> divisional Regional Transport Officers (RTOs, one per division, each with RTO-Administration and RTO-Enforcement) -> district-level Assistant Regional Transport Officers (ARTOs, typically ARTO-Administration and one or more ARTO-Enforcement per district). UP's structure uses RTO at the divisional level and ARTO at the district level, distinct from the single-tier DTO model used in some other states.
governance_bodies.subordinate_bodies: Uttar Pradesh State Road Transport Corporation (UPSRTC, public bus operator); the Transport Department is also the nodal department for the UP Road Safety Fund and (per PWD's own road-safety page) coordinates with PWD, Police and Health on the State Road Safety Council's activities.

This is an older-vintage report (2016, covering 2015-16); a more recent department-specific CAG performance audit analogous to Bihar's 2025 DTO audit was not located with confirmable content in this pass (a Transport Department chapter dated 2025 was found on cag.gov.in but its content could not be reliably extracted).

governance_bodies.name: Home Department / Uttar Pradesh Police (incl. Traffic Directorate)
governance_bodies.mandate: Overall command of law and order and traffic enforcement statewide, under the Home Department (portfolio held directly by CM Yogi Adityanath).
governance_bodies.roads_owned: None -- an enforcement body, not a road-owning one. Enforcement decisions (checkpoints, helmet drives, ITMS camera siting) are made at ADG (Traffic & Road Safety) and district SSP/SP level; infrastructure decisions that police influence but don't own require joint sign-off with the road-owning department.
governance_bodies.hierarchy: Director General of Police (DGP) heads UP Police. An Additional Director General of Police heads the Traffic & Road Safety Directorate statewide. Below the state level, UP Police is organised into 8 police zones (each headed by an ADG), 18 police ranges (each headed by an IG or DIG), and district units headed by a Senior Superintendent of Police (SSP) or Superintendent of Police (SP); each district is further divided into police circles headed by a Circle Officer (CO, DSP rank; a circle typically comprises 3-5 police stations), and circles into Thanas (police stations) headed by Inspectors/Sub-Inspectors. Several large cities (Lucknow, Kanpur, Varanasi, Agra, Ghaziabad, Prayagraj, Noida, and others) have been converted to the Police Commissionerate system, under which a Commissioner of Police holds magisterial as well as policing powers, distinct from the district-SSP model used elsewhere in the state.
governance_bodies.subordinate_bodies: Traffic & Road Safety Directorate; State Disaster Response Force (SDRF), organisationally a Police unit rather than reporting to UPSDMA directly (see UPSDMA entry); UP Police Academy and training establishments.

governance_bodies.name: Rural Development Department, Uttar Pradesh Rural Road Development Agency (UPRRDA) and Rural Engineering Department (UPRED)
governance_bodies.mandate: Rural infrastructure and PMGSY (Pradhan Mantri Gram Sadak Yojana) implementation. UPRRDA is the state's formally designated nodal/implementing agency for PMGSY in Uttar Pradesh, operating under the Rural Development Department. The Rural Engineering Department (UPRED), established 1972, is a separate technical/engineering agency historically tasked with rural (and some urban) engineering works.
governance_bodies.roads_owned: Rural roads equivalent to Other District Roads (ODR) and Village Roads (VR) elsewhere -- built and maintained via PMGSY (Union+State Centrally Sponsored Scheme) and any state-funded equivalent schemes; the specific state-funded scheme name/budget line for UP (an MMGSY-equivalent) was not established from the sources reviewed in this pass.
governance_bodies.hierarchy: Deputy CM Keshav Prasad Maurya (Minister, Rural Development) and MoS Vijay Laxmi Gautam -> Rural Development Department Secretary/Principal Secretary (not independently named in this pass) -> UPRRDA (as the PMGSY nodal/coordinating agency, with District Programme Implementation Units, DPIUs, headed by an Executive Engineer in each district) -> executing agencies, which per national PMGSY guidelines may include UPRRDA's own technical staff, the Rural Engineering Department (UPRED), or other empanelled technical agencies.
governance_bodies.subordinate_bodies: Uttar Pradesh Rural Road Development Agency (UPRRDA) -- the PMGSY nodal agency, responsible for programme coordination across departments, state-level quality control, maintenance-policy development for the PMGSY Core Network, and uniform reporting across executing agencies; Rural Engineering Department (UPRED, est. 1972).

governance_bodies.name: Panchayati Raj Institutions (PRIs), Uttar Pradesh
governance_bodies.mandate: Rural local self-government under the United Provinces Panchayat Raj Act, 1947 (Gram Panchayats) and the Uttar Pradesh Kshettra Panchayats and Zila Panchayats Adhiniyam, 1961 (the two higher tiers), both amended to conform to the 73rd Constitutional Amendment.
governance_bodies.roads_owned: Very limited -- Gram Panchayats can maintain purely internal village streets/drains where GP funds (15th Finance Commission grants, MGNREGA convergence, own tax revenue) allow; cannot independently execute PMGSY-scale road construction, which the state government (via UPRRDA) retains responsibility for even on roads serving Panchayat areas.
governance_bodies.hierarchy: Three tiers: Gram Panchayat (village level), Kshettra Panchayat (block level; historically called Kshetra Samiti), and Zila Panchayat (district level; historically called Zila Parishad). The state's own Panchayati Raj Department page lists 75 Zila Panchayats as the district-level count, consistent with UP's 75 administrative districts.
governance_bodies.subordinate_bodies: Elected political heads: Pradhan (Gram Panchayat), Block Pramukh (Kshettra Panchayat), Adhyaksha (Zila Panchayat). Administrative/executive counterparts report up the state administrative line (Panchayati Raj Department -> Director -> district cadre), not to the elected head, mirroring the pattern documented in other states.

governance_bodies.name: Urban Development Department and Urban Local Bodies (Nagar Nigams, Nagar Palika Parishads, Nagar Panchayats) and Development Authorities
governance_bodies.mandate: The Urban Development Department sets urban policy and oversees Urban Local Bodies (ULBs), constituted under the Uttar Pradesh Municipal Corporations Act, 1959 (for Nagar Nigams/Municipal Corporations) and the UP Municipalities Act, 1916 (for Nagar Palika Parishads/Nagar Panchayats); separately, Development Authorities (constituted under the UP Urban Planning and Development Act, 1973) handle land-use planning and new-area development for major cities -- e.g. Lucknow Development Authority (LDA), Kanpur Development Authority (KDA, formed 1973), Agra Development Authority (ADA), Varanasi Development Authority (VDA), Ghaziabad Development Authority (GDA), and the separately statute-constituted New Okhla Industrial Development Authority (NOIDA) and Greater Noida Industrial Development Authority (GNIDA), both under the UP Industrial Area Development Act 1976 (the same Act underpinning UPEIDA).
governance_bodies.roads_owned: Municipal roads within ULB limits: 17 Municipal Corporations (Nagar Nigams) including Lucknow, Kanpur, Varanasi, Agra, Ghaziabad and Prayagraj, plus Municipal Councils and Nagar Panchayats statewide, own and maintain roads within their limits; Development Authorities own/plan roads within their development-scheme areas until handover to the relevant ULB, a handover that (per the pattern documented in other states' development-authority relationships) is frequently delayed.
governance_bodies.hierarchy: Cabinet Minister A.K. Sharma (Urban Development & Energy) -> Principal Secretary, Urban Development -> Directorate of Local Bodies (for Nagar Nigams/Councils/Panchayats) and separately the individual Development Authorities (each with its own Vice-Chairman/CEO, typically an IAS officer, and a Chairman who in some cases is the Divisional Commissioner or another senior state appointee). Each Nagar Nigam has an elected wing (Mayor plus ward councillors) and a separate administrative wing headed by a Municipal Commissioner (an IAS or senior PCS officer appointed by the state government, not answerable to the elected Mayor for personnel matters) -- e.g. Lucknow Municipal Corporation (LMC) is headed administratively by an IAS-rank Municipal Commissioner with full executive powers, operating alongside but organisationally separate from LDA.
governance_bodies.subordinate_bodies: Directorate of Local Bodies; State Urban Development Agency (SUDA); Uttar Pradesh Jal Nigam (water/sewerage); the individual Development Authorities (LDA, KDA, ADA, VDA, GDA, NOIDA, GNIDA, and others for each major city) function as parastatal bodies distinct from -- and sometimes overlapping in jurisdiction with -- the Nagar Nigams.

governance_bodies.decision_making_power: As in other states, ULB autonomy is legally constrained -- the state government retains monitoring, inspection and rule-making powers over ULBs under the relevant Municipal Corporations/Municipalities Acts. Development Authorities exercise planning/land-use control independent of the ULB within their notified areas, which is the single largest source of the multi-agency overlap documented below.

governance_bodies.performance_issues: Overlap risk: for a single street in a city like Lucknow or Noida, the Nagar Nigam may own the carriageway/footpath, a Development Authority (LDA, NOIDA, GNIDA) may control an arterial stretch or land-use/setback rules along the frontage, and city Traffic Police controls signalling/enforcement -- a single 'fix this junction' request can require sign-off from three or more institutions, mirroring the pattern documented in Bihar's Patna case. UP's Development Authority landscape is unusually large and fragmented (a distinct authority per major city, plus NOIDA/GNIDA as separate industrial-development authorities), which this pass judges likely increases -- though does not have direct quantified evidence for -- this coordination burden relative to states with fewer or more consolidated development authorities.

governance_bodies.name: Health & Family Welfare Department, Emergency Response & Trauma Care
governance_bodies.mandate: Institutional home for pre-hospital emergency medical response and trauma care, operating through the National Health Mission, Uttar Pradesh (UPNRHM) for scheme implementation, including the 108 (Emergency Medical Transport Service, EMTS) and 102 (patient-referral/maternal-child) ambulance services, and the Uttar Pradesh Trauma and Emergency Network (UPTEN).
governance_bodies.roads_owned: None (health/trauma-care role, not road ownership).
governance_bodies.hierarchy: Deputy CM Brajesh Pathak (Minister, Health & Family Welfare and Medical Education) -> Principal Secretary/Additional Chief Secretary, Health -> Mission Director, NHM-UP -> district Chief Medical Officer (CMO, the district's senior health official and in-charge of the District Hospital, relevant to trauma-centre coordination and post-mortem/medico-legal processes after fatal crashes).
governance_bodies.subordinate_bodies: National Health Mission, Uttar Pradesh (UPNRHM), which runs the EMTS/108 and NAS/102 ambulance contracts (organised into East and West geographic clusters for 108, with separate operator agreements per a Government Order dated 14 June 2017); Ziqitza Healthcare Limited won the tender to operate UP's Advanced Life Support (ALS) '108' service in 2021, succeeding GVK EMRI, whose contract in UP ended in 2020 for lack of continued financial support.

governance_bodies.data_role: Presumptively one of the core stakeholder departments (alongside Police, Transport, and the road-owning agency) feeding hospital-side data into iRAD/e-DAR, by the pattern documented in other states; not independently confirmed for UP in this pass.
governance_bodies.performance_issues: Per an official April 2025 statement from the NHM-UP Mission Director, UP's combined 102/108/ALS ambulance fleet stood at 4,845 vehicles (2,270 under 102, 375 ALS, 2,200 under 108); average 108 response time was reported to have fallen from 28.12 minutes (2014) to 7.25 minutes (2025), and ALS response time from 30 minutes (2014) to 6.31 minutes (2025), with the 108 service reported to have assisted over 3.57 crore people over eight years. These are official-source-attributed figures reported via mainstream press rather than a primary government document reviewed directly in this pass, and should be treated accordingly (tier-4 sourcing per this project's source policy). UPTEN's rollout status/completion percentage against its 173-unit target was not established from the sources reviewed.

governance_bodies.name: Uttar Pradesh State Disaster Management Authority (UPSDMA)
governance_bodies.mandate: Constituted under the Disaster Management Act, 2005 (applied to UP via the state's own disaster-management framework) as the apex state body for disaster policy, planning and coordination; institutionally linked to mass-casualty response (major bus/truck crashes, pile-ups, bridge collapses) rather than routine single-vehicle crash response, which sits with Police/Health.
governance_bodies.roads_owned: None.
governance_bodies.hierarchy: Chairman: Chief Minister Yogi Adityanath (by statute, the standard pattern for State Disaster Management Authorities under the Disaster Management Act 2005). Vice-Chairman: Lt. Gen. Yogendra Dimri, AVSM (since on or about 15 January 2024, succeeding Lt. Gen. Ravindra Pratap Sahi, AVSM, who served 2018-2024). A CEO/Member-Secretary post exists per the Authority's standard organisational documents, but a specific current named officeholder was not confirmed via a working primary source in this pass (the Authority's own website returned repeated server errors).
governance_bodies.subordinate_bodies: State Disaster Response Force (SDRF) -- notably, UP's SDRF is organised as a unit of UP Police (headquartered in Lucknow, with Regional Response Centres across Western, Central and Eastern zones covering Bareilly/Moradabad, Lucknow/Etawah, and Ayodhya/Prayagraj/Mirzapur/Varanasi/Gorakhpur respectively) rather than reporting directly to UPSDMA -- a structural point worth flagging since it differs from a model where SDRF reports through the disaster-management authority itself. UP Police's own SDRF page explicitly lists "Road Accident" and "Train Accident" among the disaster categories SDRF responds to, alongside flood, earthquake, fire, and chemical/biological/radiological/nuclear incidents; Aapda Mitra (community-volunteer first-responder training) also operates in the state as part of the national programme.

governance_bodies.decision_making_power: The Management Committee controls Fund expenditure. Funding sources: 50% of the amount collected in any financial year through compounding of offences under the Motor Vehicles Act by the Police and Transport Departments is deposited into the Fund via budget provision in the following financial year, plus financial contributions from the UP Government or Government of India. Permitted uses: road signage and traffic signals; accident-data management systems; ambulance services; corrective measures at accident-prone locations (black spots); traffic-enforcement equipment; driving-test tracks; vehicle-inspection facilities; and traffic-safety-education programmes. Explicit restriction: Fund monies may never be placed in fixed-deposit schemes or used to extend loans.

A significant proportion of UP's official .gov.in and .nic.in domains (uppwd.gov.in, sdma.up.gov.in, upsdma.up.nic.in, upred.gov.in) returned persistent HTTP 503 errors across repeated fetch attempts in this session, despite being successfully indexed and quoted by web search; where a specific fact could only be sourced to such a domain via a search-engine snippet rather than a direct, rendered fetch, this is disclosed in the relevant confidence note rather than silently presented as a directly-verified read. district_level_actors.Role: Presumptive chair of the District Road Safety Committee per the MV Act 215(3) national template; controls land acquisition for road projects; top-most official of revenue and civil administration in the district (IAS cadre), assisted by ADMs, with the district divided into subdivisions headed by Sub-Divisional Magistrates (SDMs).

district_level_actors.Actor: Senior Superintendent of Police / Superintendent of Police (SSP/SP), or Commissioner of Police in Commissionerate cities
district_level_actors.Role: Heads district (or city) law-and-order and traffic enforcement. In Commissionerate cities (Lucknow, Kanpur, Varanasi, Agra, Ghaziabad, Prayagraj, Noida, and others converted to this system), the Commissioner of Police holds magisterial as well as policing powers, replacing the DM/SSP dual structure for policing matters within city limits.

District-level licensing, registration, permits and enforcement (Administration and Enforcement postings); reports up to the divisional Regional Transport Officer (RTO). UP's two-tier RTO(divisional)/ARTO(district) structure differs from a single-tier DTO model used in some other states.
The engineering decision-maker for SH/MDR design changes, signage, and maintenance within the district.

district_level_actors.Actor: Executive Engineer, UPRRDA (District Programme Implementation Unit)
district_level_actors.Role: The engineering decision-maker for PMGSY-funded rural-road (ODR/VR) works within the district; heads the District Programme Implementation Unit (DPIU) per national PMGSY guidelines.

District's senior health official and in-charge of the District Hospital; relevant to trauma-centre readiness and post-mortem/medico-legal processes after fatal crashes. UP's official district portals (e.g. mau.nic.in, kanpurnagar.nic.in) list a named CMO for each district.

Where the district headquarters or another town is a Nagar Nigam/Nagar Palika Parishad/Nagar Panchayat, controls municipal roads within town limits; the Municipal Commissioner (Nagar Nigam) is a state-appointed IAS/PCS officer with executive powers independent of the elected Mayor.

District-level rural body (75 statewide, one per district); the elected Adhyaksha chairs the body, while an administrative executive (reporting up the state Panchayati Raj cadre line, per the pattern documented in other states) carries out day-to-day functions.

Replicate the DM/SP relationship at subdivision/circle level -- the CO (DSP rank) typically heads a police circle of 3-5 police stations; useful when a problem is very localised and doesn't need full-district escalation.

bihar.political_context: Bihar held Legislative Assembly elections in November 2025, and the state's government changed hands in April–May 2026: Nitish Kumar's uninterrupted run as Chief Minister ended on 15 April 2026, and Samrat Choudhary (BJP) was sworn in as the 24th Chief Minister the same day, with the full cabinet reshuffled and portfolios allocated on 7–8 May 2026. As of the most recent verification (9 September 2026), Samrat Choudhary was confirmed still actively functioning as CM through contemporaneous press coverage of his public appearances (felicitating students, attending public events). Under the 8 May 2026 portfolio allocation, the CM retains Home, General Administration, Vigilance, Election, Civil Aviation and unallocated departments; Deputy CM Vijay Kumar Chaudhary holds Water Resources & Parliamentary Affairs; Deputy CM Bijendra Prasad Yadav holds Finance & Commercial Taxes; Road Construction went to Kumar Shailendra; and Energy went to Shailesh Kumar ("Bulo Mandal"). This is a structural change with direct road-safety consequences: the Transport Minister (now Damodar Rawat), the Road Construction Minister (now Kumar Shailendra), and both Deputy Chief Ministers are all different people than a year ago, meaning most of Bihar's road-safety-relevant political leadership is newly in role and has, by definition, no track record yet in its current position. Underlying this political layer, India's constitutional Seventh Schedule splits road-related subjects across the Union and State Lists, and because roads, transport and police all sit substantially on the State List (with the Union retaining National Highways, the overarching Motor Vehicles Act framework, and centrally sponsored schemes like PMGSY), Bihar's state government and its departments are the primary point of leverage for almost all road-safety interventions CrashFree India will pursue — the Union government matters mainly for NH stretches, PMGSY funding rules, and the national legal framework. Additionally, this pass resolved a previously unnamed gap: the 7–8 May 2026 cabinet expansion allocated the Health portfolio to Nishant Kumar, son of former CM and JD(U) national president Nitish Kumar, his first ministerial appointment (LatestLY, Republic World, Daily Pioneer) — relevant background given JD(U)’s continuing weight in the coalition despite Nitish Kumar himself now sitting in the Rajya Sabha.

governance_bodies.decision_making_power: Can suspend/cancel driving licences, register/deregister vehicles, grant/deny permits, levy tax and penalties administratively. Policy changes to MV Rules require State Cabinet/Legislature notification; major enforcement-technology procurement (e.g. ITMS cameras) is coordinated with the Home Department/Traffic Police.
governance_bodies.data_role: Holds the vehicle registration database (VAHAN) and driving licence database (SARATHI), permit records; one of the four core data-contributing departments to iRAD/e-DAR.
governance_bodies.performance_issues: A 2025 CAG performance audit of District Transport Offices in Bihar found irregularities in driving-skill testing, licence issuance, and vehicle registration compliance, examining organisational structure/functions of DTOs and covering issuance of learner and driving licences, driving-skill-testing infrastructure inadequacies, and registration/permit irregularities.
governance_bodies.meeting_frequency: Not specified beyond Road Safety Council/DRSC cadence covered elsewhere in this document.

governance_bodies.name: Road Construction Department (RCD)
governance_bodies.mandate: A premier works department conducting planning, designing, construction, improvement, strengthening and maintenance of roads and bridges — including flyovers, ROBs (rail-over-bridges) and elevated corridors.
governance_bodies.roads_owned: State Highways (SH), Major District Roads (MDR), and National Highways segments not entrusted to NHAI (the "NH Wing, RCD" roads — historically the majority of Bihar's NH length; NHAI directly holds a smaller, growing share as projects are handed over).
governance_bodies.hierarchy: Secretary (IAS) → Engineer-in-Chief (E-in-C) for technical matters (with a separate Additional Secretary/Joint Secretary line for personnel/admin) → eight Wings, each headed by a Chief Engineer (CE) → Circles → Divisions → Sub-Divisions, following the standard PWD-style "Wing–Circle–Division–Sub-Division" hierarchy.
governance_bodies.subordinate_bodies: Bihar State Road Development Corporation (BSRDC) — a public limited company fully owned by the Government of Bihar, established in 2009 to promote surface infrastructure by taking up road works, bridges, widening, strengthening and maintenance of roads — and Bihar Rajya Pul Nirman Nigam Ltd (BRPNNL), both reporting to the RCD Secretary; not shown in the department's main organogram but report to the Secretary, RCD.

governance_bodies.decision_making_power: Technical sanction of state road/bridge projects, contractor debarment, day-to-day maintenance decisions on SH/MDR. Land acquisition needs district revenue machinery; large projects need Finance Department budget sanction and often Cabinet approval; NH works funded/sanctioned by MoRTH still need MoRTH clearance even when executed by the NH Wing.
governance_bodies.data_role: Acts as the road-owning-agency stakeholder in iRAD's engineer-alert workflow for design review after crashes on SH/MDR/NH-not-with-NHAI roads.
governance_bodies.performance_issues: A section of the Vikramshila Bridge in Bhagalpur collapsed in 2026, after which the executive engineer responsible for the bridge's maintenance was suspended pending investigation; a string of earlier collapses led the Supreme Court to issue notices to the Bihar government, NHAI, the RCD Additional Chief Secretary, the BRPNNL chairperson, and the Rural Works Department Additional Chief Secretary, on a PIL seeking a structural audit of the state's bridges.
governance_bodies.meeting_frequency: Not specified.

governance_bodies.name: Rural Works Department (RWD)
governance_bodies.mandate: Responsible for construction of rural roads with necessary culverts and cross-drainage structures.
governance_bodies.roads_owned: Other District Roads (ODR) and Village Roads (VR), with the objective of improving "Farm to Market Connectivity"; implements PMGSY (Pradhan Mantri Gram Sadak Yojana, a Centrally Sponsored Scheme) and state-funded equivalents — Mukhya Mantri Gram Sadak Yojana (MMGSY, launched 2013–14), MMGSY (Remaining) (launched 2023), and the Gramin Tola Sampark Nischay Yojana.
governance_bodies.hierarchy: Structure parallel to RCD: Engineer-in-Chief (RWD), Chief Engineers, Superintending Engineers, Executive Engineers at Circle/Division level. RWD's internal Wing/Circle organisational structure was not found in as much organogram detail as RCD's (a carried-over gap).
governance_bodies.subordinate_bodies: Not always executed by RWD's own engineering staff — in the initial 2000s ramp-up, the Government of Bihar asked the Ministry of Rural Development to engage central agencies, and tripartite agreements were signed with IRCON International, National Buildings Construction Corporation, National Hydroelectric Power Corporation and National Projects Construction Corporation, along with CPWD, covering 33 of Bihar's 37 districts at the time.

governance_bodies.decision_making_power: Holds the engineering and budgetary machinery for construction/maintenance even on roads that serve individual villages; under PMGSY-III, "responsibility of construction and maintenance of PMGSY works lies with the state government" (i.e., RWD), not the local body, even though the roads serve local body areas.
governance_bodies.data_role: Acts as the road-owning-agency stakeholder in iRAD for ODR/VR crash-site design review.
governance_bodies.performance_issues: PMGSY has a three-tier quality monitoring system — internal QC by contractors at the project level, a second tier of independent State Quality Monitors inspecting in three stages, and a third tier of National Quality Monitors carrying out random field inspections and grading execution quality.
governance_bodies.meeting_frequency: Progress of PMGSY is reviewed through Regional Review Meetings, Performance Review Committee meetings, and Empowered Committee meetings with states, plus Bihar's own internal reviews. RWD's 2025–26 budget of ₹11,101.64 crore was presented to the Assembly, reporting 764 km of MMGSY roads built in 2024–25 and a target of a further 8,600 km in 2025–26, alongside 700 new rural bridges planned for the year.

governance_bodies.name: Panchayati Raj Institutions (PRIs)
governance_bodies.mandate: Rural local self-government under the Bihar Panchayat Raj Act, 2006, implementing the 73rd Constitutional Amendment.
governance_bodies.roads_owned: Very limited — Gram Panchayats can maintain purely internal village streets/drains where GP funds (15th Finance Commission grants, MGNREGA convergence, own tax revenue) allow; cannot independently execute PMGSY/MMGSY-scale road construction.
governance_bodies.hierarchy: Three tiers: Gram Panchayat (GP) at village level, Panchayat Samiti at Block level, and Zila Parishad at District level — at present 8,053 Gram Panchayats, 533 Panchayat Samitis and 38 Zila Parishads are functional, with Gram Panchayats divided into roughly 1.15 lakh wards. A Gram Kachahry (village-level dispute-resolution body) exists at each GP; a Ward Sabha exists at each ward under the Ward Member, alongside the Gram Sabha at GP level.
governance_bodies.subordinate_bodies: Elected political heads: Mukhiya (GP), Pramukh (Panchayat Samiti), Adhyaksha (Zila Parishad). Administrative/executive counterparts: Panchayat Secretary (GP), BDO-cum-Executive Officer (Panchayat Samiti), and Deputy Development Commissioner-cum-CEO (Zila Parishad) — reporting up the state administrative line (Panchayati Raj Department → Director → district BDO/DDC cadre), not to the elected head.
governance_bodies.decision_making_power: A Gram Panchayat may impose a yearly tax on occupants of holdings, and on professions, trades, callings and employment carried on within its jurisdiction, subject to State Government approval of the maximum tax rate (Section 27, BPRA 2006); the State Government retains rule-making power (Section 146) and the power to issue model regulations and inquire into Panchayat affairs (Sections 150 and 152). Every Gram Panchayat must prepare a development plan annually and submit it to the Panchayat Samiti (Sections 166–167).
governance_bodies.data_role: PRIs have a formally recognised awareness/participation role in road safety — the 2020 amendment to Bihar's Road Safety Council Rules explicitly tasks the Transport Department's coordination committee with ensuring "active participation of Panchayati Raj Institutions, Urban Local Bodies and NGOs in road safety awareness programmes" — distinct from an engineering role.
governance_bodies.performance_issues: The state government intimated in Feb. 2005, based on department resolutions from September 2001, that functions of 20 departments had been devolved to PRIs — but a CAG review found that while activity mapping had been done, actual transfer of functions, functionaries and funds to PRIs by these departments had not fully materialised — a documented, audited gap between paper devolution and real administrative control.
governance_bodies.meeting_frequency: Annual development-plan submission cycle (Sections 166–167, BPRA 2006); Gram Sabha/Ward Sabha meetings for local matters.

governance_bodies.name: Home Department / Bihar Police (incl. Traffic Police)
governance_bodies.mandate: Overall command of law and order and traffic enforcement statewide, under the Home Department (headed politically by the Chief Minister, who traditionally also holds the Home portfolio in Bihar).
governance_bodies.roads_owned: None — an enforcement body, not a road-owning one. Enforcement decisions (checkpoint locations, helmet/seatbelt drives, drunk-driving campaigns) are made at ADG (Traffic) and district SP level; infrastructure decisions that police influence but don't own (camera placement, signal timing, physical traffic-calming) require joint sign-off with the Transport Department and/or the road-owning engineering department.
governance_bodies.hierarchy: Director General of Police (DGP) heads Bihar Police. An Additional Director General of Police (ADG), Traffic heads traffic policing statewide; district-level traffic enforcement is typically headed by an SP (Traffic) in major cities (e.g., Patna) or handled by the general district SP/SSP elsewhere, with Traffic DSPs and Traffic Inspectors/Sub-Inspectors at the operational level. Bihar has 43 Police Districts (headed by SP/SSP) and 853 Police Stations; a Police District is divided into Police Subdivisions headed by a DSP. Patna and other large cities have designated City SPs (e.g., SP City East/West) separate from rural SPs, plus a dedicated SP (Traffic), Patna.
governance_bodies.subordinate_bodies: Crime Investigation Department (CID) for serious/fatal hit-and-run or negligence cases; Economic Offences Unit; Bihar Police Academy and Constable Training School/Military Police training centres.

governance_bodies.decision_making_power: ADG (Traffic) Sudhanshu Kumar issued an order restricting vehicle-checking authority to Sub-Inspector rank and above, with constables and ASIs limited to traffic management and keeping roads free of congestion — illustrating direct operational rule-making power over how enforcement is conducted statewide.
governance_bodies.data_role: Police are the first-entry stakeholder for both FIR/crime records and the iRAD/e-DAR crash database; once police enter accident details with photos/videos and a unique ID is created, an alert automatically goes to a PWD/local-body engineer under iRAD's design.
governance_bodies.performance_issues: The Transport Department has directed all DTOs to identify roughly 700 sites for an Integrated Traffic Management System (ITMS), with the State Transport Commissioner instructing that site selection be carried out in coordination with Traffic Police for technical accuracy.

governance_bodies.name: Urban Development & Housing Department (UDHD) and Urban Local Bodies
governance_bodies.mandate: UDHD sets urban policy; its principal implementing arm for infrastructure is BUIDCO (Bihar Urban Infrastructure Development Corporation), established 2009 under the Companies Act 1956, functioning as the apex body for planning, coordination and implementation of urban development projects (water supply, sewerage, urban transport, housing, solid waste management).
governance_bodies.roads_owned: Municipal roads within Urban Local Body limits (Nagar Nigams/Municipal Corporations, Nagar Parishads/Municipal Councils, Nagar Panchayats) under the Bihar Municipal Act, 2007 — as of April 2026 there were 264 Urban Local Bodies in the state. Patna Municipal Corporation (PMC, established 1952) handles municipal roads, drains, streetlights within Patna.
governance_bodies.hierarchy: Each ULB has an elected wing (Mayor for Corporations, Chairperson for Councils, President for Nagar Panchayats, plus ward councillors) and a separate administrative wing; day-to-day execution runs through a Municipal Commissioner (Corporations) or Executive Officer (Councils/Nagar Panchayats), state cadre officers not directly under the elected Mayor's control for personnel matters.
governance_bodies.subordinate_bodies: BUIDCO; the Patna Metropolitan Area Authority (PMAA) — the current metropolitan planning body, constituted under the Bihar Urban Planning & Development Act, 2012, as successor to the defunct Patna Regional Development Authority (PRDA, established 1979, dissolved 2007 when the Bihar Municipal Act, 2007 repealed its enabling legislation).

governance_bodies.decision_making_power: The Bihar Municipal Act 2007 gives the State Government powers to monitor ULB functioning, with decision-making on all key issues ultimately resting with the state and ULBs having only some powers over service delivery; government may inspect any ULB office or call for its records — i.e., ULB autonomy is legally constrained.
governance_bodies.data_role: ULB engineer is the "Road" stakeholder in iRAD for municipal-road crashes.
governance_bodies.performance_issues: Overlap risk: for a single Patna street, PMC may own the carriageway/footpath, RCD/BSRDC may own a flyover/arterial stretch, Traffic Police controls signalling/enforcement, and a development authority (e.g. PMAA) may control land-use/setback rules along the frontage — a single "fix this junction" request can require sign-off from three or four institutions.
governance_bodies.meeting_frequency: PMC's Empowered Standing Committee (its key internal decision body) has directed executive officers and ward councillors to make daily ward visits to resolve complaints on roads, drainage and streetlights on the spot.

governance_bodies.name: Health Department, Emergency Response & Trauma Care
governance_bodies.mandate: Institutional home for trauma care and emergency medical response, operating through the State Health Society, Bihar (SHSB) for scheme implementation.
governance_bodies.roads_owned: None (health/trauma-care role, not road ownership).
governance_bodies.hierarchy: Minister, Health; Principal Secretary/Additional Chief Secretary, Health; Executive Director, SHSB; Civil Surgeon (district-level health officer, relevant to trauma-centre coordination and medico-legal/post-mortem processes after fatal crashes).
governance_bodies.subordinate_bodies: State Health Society, Bihar (SHSB) — provides pre-hospital care via Advanced Life Saving Ambulances (108 service) piloted under Public-Private Partnership.

governance_bodies.decision_making_power: Directed, alongside the Transport Department, to operationalise integration of private ambulances into the unified Dial 112 emergency helpline; directed for 11 upgraded trauma centres to have ICU operations running by mid-2026 (a target that appears to have slipped — as of 1 July 2026, a month past deadline, still described as forward-looking plans, with no later confirmation found that rollout has since been completed).
governance_bodies.data_role: One of the four core stakeholder departments (alongside Police, Transport, and the road-owning agency) feeding hospital-side data into iRAD/e-DAR.
governance_bodies.performance_issues: Bihar currently has around 3,700 ambulances (government and private combined), of which only about 2,000 operate under the government system; national standards recommend a 10-minute ambulance response, but Bihar's average is around 25 minutes — a documented, quantified capacity gap directly relevant to post-crash survivability. 55 hospitals are designated trauma centres (10 Level Two, 35 Level Three, 10 integrated trauma-and-emergency facilities).
governance_bodies.meeting_frequency: Not specified.

governance_bodies.name: Disaster Management Department / Bihar State Disaster Management Authority (BSDMA)
governance_bodies.mandate: Institutionally linked to mass-casualty response (e.g., major bus/truck crashes, bridge collapses) rather than routine single-vehicle crash response, which sits with Police/Health; copied on Bihar's Road Safety Council notifications as a stakeholder.
governance_bodies.roads_owned: None.
governance_bodies.hierarchy: Not detailed beyond BSDMA/Disaster Management Department structure.
governance_bodies.subordinate_bodies: State Disaster Response Force (SDRF); Aapda Mitra ("disaster friend") volunteer scheme.
governance_bodies.decision_making_power: Runs "Safety Weeks" (Road Safety, Earthquake Safety, Fire Safety, Flood Safety), safe-school programmes, and public IEC (information-education-communication) material distribution as part of structural and non-structural disaster-risk-reduction work; runs the Aapda Mitra volunteer scheme, under which trained community volunteers contribute to prevention, rescue work and public awareness specifically around road accidents, alongside flood and fire response.
governance_bodies.data_role: Not a core iRAD data contributor; role is concentrated in awareness campaigns and volunteer first-responder training, not road engineering, enforcement, or day-to-day single-vehicle crash response.
governance_bodies.performance_issues: Not documented.
governance_bodies.meeting_frequency: Review interactions between BSDMA, SDRF and Aapda Mitra volunteers have been reported; specific frequency not stated.

governance_bodies.name: Bihar Rajya Pul Nirman Nigam Ltd (BRPNNL) — Bridges
governance_bodies.mandate: Started in 1975 as a Bihar government undertaking under the Companies Act 1956, mandated mainly to construct bridges and roads, and now undertaking a broader range of civil engineering projects.
governance_bodies.roads_owned: Bridges (major, on SH/MDR/NH) via RCD; bridges (rural), sometimes contracted.
governance_bodies.hierarchy: Reports to the Secretary, RCD (per RCD's own organogram).
governance_bodies.subordinate_bodies: None specified.
governance_bodies.decision_making_power: Acts as the executing/engineering body for bridge-specific problems, with RCD as the political/administrative supervisor and outside technical institutions (e.g., IIT Patna) sometimes brought in for structural audits.
governance_bodies.data_role: Not specified beyond its bridge-engineering role.
governance_bodies.performance_issues: Following cracks found in the Lakhisarai bypass overbridge, a review meeting was chaired by the RCD Secretary, with technical reports jointly submitted by BRPNNL and IIT Patna.
governance_bodies.meeting_frequency: Not specified.

governance_bodies.name: Bihar Road Safety Council
governance_bodies.mandate: Constituted under Motor Vehicles Act 1988, Section 215 (enabling states to constitute road safety councils/committees), operationalised through the Bihar Road Safety Council Rules, 2018.
governance_bodies.roads_owned: None (coordination/policy body).
governance_bodies.hierarchy: Constituted at state level under the chairmanship of the Transport Minister. Secretariat/Lead Agency housed in the Transport Department (an "Executive Officer, Lead Agency, Bihar Road Safety Council" post exists, per the 2020 notification's distribution list). A key operational sub-body, the Co-Ordination Committee of Transport, was defined/amended in 2020.
governance_bodies.subordinate_bodies: Co-Ordination Committee of Transport (within the Transport Department); District Road Safety Committees at district level.

governance_bodies.decision_making_power: The Co-Ordination Committee of Transport is responsible for formulating sub-policies under the Bihar Road Safety Policy, preparing/updating the Bihar Road Safety work plan, budgetary provisions of the Road Safety Fund, legislative reforms on road safety in the transport sector, formulating/monitoring a safe school-bus policy, developing/implementing road-safety publicity campaigns (incl. annual Road Safety Week), monitoring driving-training-school and computerised-test-centre implementation, ensuring PRI/ULB/NGO participation in awareness programmes, and monitoring implementation of MV Act road-safety measures and Supreme/High Court directions.
governance_bodies.data_role: Stakeholders formally copied on Council notifications: Development Commissioner; Additional Chief Secretary, Home; Additional Chief Secretary, Road Construction; Principal Secretary, Education; Principal Secretary, Health; Principal Secretary, Disaster Management; Principal Secretary, Custom Excise & Registration; Secretary, Urban Development & Housing; Secretary, Rural Works; DG-cum-Commandant General, Home Guards & Fire Services; Additional DG, CID; Managing Director, BRPNNL; Managing Director, BSRDC; Municipal Commissioner, Patna Municipal Corporation; SP Traffic, Patna; Regional Officer, NHAI, Patna; all District Magistrates; all SSPs/SPs; all District Transport Officers — the state's own map of who it considers a road-safety stakeholder.
governance_bodies.performance_issues: The existence of a dated 2020 amendment notification, ongoing Road Safety Week observances, and school-curriculum integration (road safety chapters for classes VI–VIII from 2014–15) indicate the Council/Lead Agency structure is at least intermittently active; no direct evidence of a regular meeting cadence was found.

governance_bodies.name: District Road Safety Committees (DRSCs)
governance_bodies.mandate: MV Act Section 215(3) — the State Government constitutes a District Road Safety Committee by notification, consisting of a Chairman and other members as it considers necessary.

karnataka.political_context: Siddaramaiah resigned as Chief Minister on 28 May 2026 and D. K. Shivakumar was sworn in as the 18th Chief Minister of Karnataka on 3 June 2026, with G. Parameshwara as Deputy CM (Revenue, Youth Empowerment and Sports), under an internal Congress power-sharing arrangement whose exact terms were never formally announced. Portfolios were allocated on 4 June 2026 and reshuffled again on 27 August 2026 when the cabinet was expanded. As of Shivakumar's 100th day in office (10 September 2026, an event his predecessor Siddaramaiah himself inaugurated and publicly endorsed) he remains Chief Minister with no rotation back to Siddaramaiah having occurred, though persistent speculation about a power-sharing 'rotation' understanding means this should be re-checked before any future use of this document. Priyank Kharge became Home Minister (excluding Intelligence, which the CM retains) from the June 2026 reshuffle, with a strongly technology/digital-policing-focused agenda; Byrathi Suresh became Transport Minister, succeeding Ramalinga Reddy (who moved to Major and Medium Irrigation/Water Resources, then to Forest, Ecology and Environment on 13 August 2026 after briefly resigning over being denied the Bengaluru Development portfolio); and Satish Jarkiholi retained Public Works through the August 2026 reshuffle. The single most significant new development remains that, on 9 September 2026, the Enforcement Directorate conducted money-laundering raids at roughly 18-21 locations linked to PWD Minister Satish Jarkiholi, including his Bengaluru residence and properties tied to his MP daughter Priyanka Jarkiholi and other relatives/associates, seizing roughly Rs 3.3 crore in unaccounted cash; Chief Minister Shivakumar publicly called the raids 'politically motivated', and as of the most recent reporting located (13 September 2026) Jarkiholi remains PWD Minister with no resignation or removal reported — this is an active, fast-moving situation that could affect the stability of the PWD ministerial relationship on short notice, and no news dated after 13 September 2026 could be located despite a direct search. A second significant thread, newly surfaced in this pass, is genuine contradictory sourcing over who currently holds the state's ADGP Traffic and Road Safety post: prior reporting names both R. Hithendra (additional charge, reported June 2025) and Alok Kumar (continuously from June 2023 until his own transfer to ADGP Training around May 2026), and no confirmed successor to Alok Kumar in that specific post was located — CrashFree India should confirm this post's current holder directly before any outreach premised on it. Separately, Bengaluru's Joint Commissioner of Police (Traffic) changed hands in July 2025, from M. N. Anucheth (transferred to DIG, Recruitment) to Karthik Reddy, who has publicly framed his own mandate explicitly around improving road safety and traffic management — CrashFree India's working-level Bengaluru traffic-enforcement contact should be updated accordingly. Any reference to 'Transport Minister Ramalinga Reddy,' 'CM Siddaramaiah,' or 'Joint CP Traffic M. N. Anucheth' is now historically relevant only, not a current contact.
